maintopic: ANGLO-AMERICAN CONSULTATIONS CANADIAN REPRESENTATION-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Under standing order 31 an hon. member, desiring to move the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance rises in his place and gives notice and sends to the Speaker a statement of the reasons for his motion. The matter must be one of urgent public importance. If the matter is not in the opinion of the Speaker of such urgent public importance he may not put the motion to the house. In the suggestion made by the hon. member now I do not think there is such urgency as to justify the motion he has made; therefore I do not present it to the house.

maintopic: QUESTIONS

speechtext:
1.	Are married men under the age of thirty years eligible for enlistment in the reserve army?

Questions
2.	If so, when was the change made which enables them to enlist?
3.	Have there been any other changes since July 1, 1942, in the qualifications for enlistment in the reserve army?

maintopic: QUESTIONS
speechtext:
1.	Yes, provided they are not within the age classes designated by proclamation for military training under the national selective service mobilization regulations. Married men under the age of thirty years are therefore eligible for enlistment in the reserve army if
(a)	they are between the ages of 17 and 19;
(b)	born during the years 1917 to 1924, provided those born in 1924 have attained their nineteenth birthday and (1) they have been granted postponement of military training; or (2) they have been called but are found to be in a medical category below that prescribed as acceptable for military training under regulations made pursuant to the National Resources Mobilization Act, 1940.
(c)	they were born prior to the year 1917;
(d)	they belong to the classes of persons to whom the national selective service mobilization regulations do not apply, such as judges, clergymen, members of municipal police forces or fire brigades, etc.
(e)	students undergoing approved military training under the national selective service mobilization regulations.
2.	February 17, 1943-Canadian army order No. 86.
3.	No. The only change made by Canadian order No. 86 was to provide that all married men born prior to 1917 are now permitted to join the reserve army, whereas previously those under the age of thirty were required to be in a medical category lower than "B".

4.	Proposals relating to inventions that are received directly by the board or referred to it by government departments, are submitted to an examining committee for investigation. The committee endeavours to ascertain if the invention contains any feature of practical utility not already known to those responsible for the prosecution of the war and is empowered to seek the advice of appropriate scientific or military consultants. The consultants include members of the scientific staff of the National Research Council and specially qualified officers of the armed services. Inventions considered to be worthy of development are referred to appropriate government departments or other organizations. Inventions are rejected on the grounds of impracticability or lack of novelty, or because the invention, though sound, is not needed, is already in use, or would require too long a time to develop to the effective stage.

Its functions are to examine inventions, reject impracticable and unsound proposals and to assess the value of promising ideas and place them before the appropriate government officers. From 10 to 15 per cent of the proposals received are of such evident merit that they must be referred to the appropriate panel of consultants before a decision can be reached regarding them. About four-fifths of the proposals now being received deal with ideas which have been previously considered by the board or that are of slight technical interest but of no immediate military value.

1.	Was a survey made recently of the Ganaraska river watershed?
2.	If so, what are the findings and to what extent is the flooding of that river in springtime caused by the dams built and owned by private individuals and industrial corporations?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: QUESTIONS
speechtext:
The survey of the Ganaraska river watershed is still in progress, and only an interim report will be available at the end of the present fiscal year. The final report will include chapters on all the physical features of the area, and on all aspects of conservation and employment projects. At least one of these chapters will assemble such information as is

Questions as Orders for Returns
available on the flooding of the river, both in the past and at present; but this chapter has not yet been written.
The survey is a cooperative project in which staff of the provincial government and of the dominion government are each making contributions; but the direction of the actual field survey, and the preparation of the final report, are in the charge of the chairman of the interdepartmental committee on conservation and rehabilitation of the Ontario government.
The objectives of the survey are referred to in P.C. 97/8097, September 9, 1942, which authorizes the dominion share of the financing, as follows:
(i)	To ascertain in detail the measures and techniques needed for the rehabilitation of this deteriorated area.
(ii)	To evaluate the amount of employment which can be provided by the conservation projects required to rehabilitate this area.
(iii)	In general, to serve as a demonstration study and a yardstick by which other areas in Canada could be appraised for similar purposes.

speechtext:
Order. The matter of asking questions on the orders of the day was discussed last week. The hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) has now asked whether the Minister of National Revenue is in a position to make a statement respecting policy in his department. This is a question of the kind which I have said hitherto should be placed on the order paper. I should like to state more clearly what the position is respecting questions asked on the orders of the day.
The attention of the house ought to be drawn to the growing practice of asking, when the orders of the day are called, oral questions which should be placed on the order paper.
We must not forget that putting questions to the ministers at that phase of the day's proceedings is not allowed here by any rule, whilst in the United Kingdom house an hour is set aside for questions under a special standing order, which also requires that-
-notice of any such question must appear at latest on the notice paper circulated on the day before that on which an answer is desired.
On that point May, at page 243, says:
After private business has been disposed of, and not later than three o'clock on Mondays, Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Thursdays, the Speaker calls on the members who have given notices of questions to which oral answers are

Questions on Orders of the Day
desired, but.no questions can be taken after a quarter to four o'clock, except questions which have not been answered in consequence of the absence of the minister to whom they are addressed, and questions which have not appeared on the paper, but which are of an urgent character and relate either to matters of public importance or to the arrangement of business. As each member is called, he rises to ask the question, standing in his name; but in case the member responsible for a question does not answer to the Speaker's call, a minister may rise and make such statement upon the question as the public interest demands.
As long as our standing orders are unchanged, the only questions permitted on the orders of the day being called must be confined to very urgent matters, personal explanations, inaccurate reports of speeches delivered in the house, denial of charges, dilatoriness in obtaining returns, or other similar matters closely connected with the routine business of the house. These questions must be brief and must not be prefaced by any argument. Standing order 44 gives members ample opportunity to place on the order paper any number of questions they desire with respect to public affairs. Reading telegrams, letters or extracts from newspapers as an opening to a question when the orders of the day are called is an abuse of the rules of the house. It is not good parliamentary practice to communicate written allegations to the house and then to ask ministers either to confirm or to deny them. It is the member's duty to ascertain the truth of any statement before he brings it to the attention of parliament. This has been decided long ago in the United Kingdom House of Commons. On June 14, 1882, Mr. Speaker Brand, in preventing a member from reading a telegram from a newspaper and founding a question on it, pointed out the extreme inconvenience of founding questions on every telegram in every newspaper. "I am bound to say," he added, "that it does appear to me that before questions of . such gravity are put, an hon. member should take some measures to ascertain the truth of the telegram." This quotation is from Denison's and Brand's Decisions, page 230.
I feel it is my duty to explain to the house the procedure with regard to questions, and I hope that in applying it I shall have the cooperation of all members of the house.

Mr. Speaker, I wanted to refer to a report in a Toronto paper of the speech made by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) at the annual meeting of the Dominion Progressive Conservative association on Saturday. The portion of the report to which I should like to refer reads:
Canadian military officers wished to send a contingent to participate in the North African campaign but lack of reinforcements prevented it, Hon. W. Earl Rowe, M.P., hinted at the annual meeting of the Dominion Progressive Conservative association held here to-day.
"To-day we have the humiliation of listening to rumours that many military officers wanted our forces to enter the African battles but it was not possible because there were not sufficient reinforcements over there," said Mr. Rowe.
I just want to say that the statement or the rumour or the suggestion that it was not possible for Canadians to participate in North Africa because of insufficient reinforcements is without foundation in fact. The composition of the force for North Africa was determined by those who had the responsibility for allied strategy in Europe and who were in a position to judge what employment of allied troops, both for these and for other tasks, would best serve the common cause. From personal inquiries which I made when I was over there I am quite satisfied that their decision in respect to the composition of this force was based upon that principle.

Tasks of tracing evaders is to be carried on by Associated Credit Bureaus of Canada Limited, an organization with some 58 offices across the country.
My comment on that was that there was no truth in it. Actually the answer I gave my hon. friend was correct, because we have not made any definite arrangements with the Associated Credit Bureaus of Canada or any similar organization to trace evaders under
The Budget-Mr. Perley

the National Resources Mobilization Act. It is a fact, however, that consideration is being given to the possibility of using any organization there may be in Canada already established for tracing the addresses of people who cannot be found. The national selective service officials are studying the matter, and if a plan of this kind can be developed usefully and with less expense to the dominion government it certainly will be given careful consideration. It goes without saying that we are using every possible avenue to trace those who may be delinquent under the National Resources Mobilization Act. We are making use of the names compiled by credit agencies, street directories, telephone directories and in fact any other information available. Up to the present this work has been done by special staffs employed for this purpose. If we find that we can use existing agencies effectively and with less expense we will do so.
It is my desire at all times to give hon. members of this house all the information I can, and the correct information. Therefore in fairness to the hon. member for Lake Centre, I felt I should make this statement to the house.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think I can be charged with having taken up too much time of the house this session, but as you accorded me the adjournment of the debate on Friday last I should like to make a few observations and one or two constructive suggestions on the budget.
This is a war budget. We might be asked, what are we going to do about it? So far as the opposition is concerned I think the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) set out clearly what we are going to do about it. Since no amendment was moved by the opposition, this budget of course is going through so far as we are concerned. The hon. member for Danforth reviewed in detail and in a very moderate tone the proposals of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) and

offered some constructive suggestions. I commend his speech to every reader of Hansard in Canada. Since he covered the subject so well it remains for me only to refer to the budget in so far as it affects the province of Saskatchewan, one of the constituencies of which I have the honour to represent.
Like every other budget, this one contains some good features and others that are not so good. The minister budgeted for a deficit, not for a surplus. But we are at war, and that deficit will have to be met in some way. It may be taken up by the people in loans, and perhaps a supplementary estimate will also be brought down. But the winning of the war is the first and all-important thing for this house to consider. I am sure that the Canadian people are willing to pay any taxes that may be necessary and do anything within reason to win the war.
The Minister of Finance in presenting his budget said that his income tax proposals contained no very great changes. But when you come to dissect those proposals, Mr. Speaker, you find that we have to pay two and a half years' income taxes within two years and that $105,000,000 more is to be extracted from the people of Canada this year, at the same rate of taxation, than was taken from them last year. As I have said, the people of Canada are willing to pay any taxes that may be necessary, but certainly they want to be assured that in the expenditure of this money there will be no extravagance and no graft and that every cent will be expended carefully.
There are three main problems before the country. First there is labour; second, the soldier; and third, industry. Much has already been said and more will be said about labour; therefore I shall not dwell on that; suffice it to say that labour undoubtedly has the right of association and the right to organize. Labour has also the right, and the people of Canada expect it of them, to give a full day's work for a full day's pay, and to receive fair treatment. I shall refer to labour a little later in connection with the farm labour shortage.
Next is the problem of the soldier, not only the soldier in the armed forces here and overseas, and the question of reinforcements, but the question of taking care of the soldiers when they return from the war.
Industry is the third factor, and I refer to agriculture in particular because I think it plays the .most important part in the industrial life of Canada to-day. The minister said that so far as taxes are concerned

The Budget-Mr. Perley
the farmer does not fare too badly. I shall refer to that later. What I wish to say at the moment is that both during the war-and it is not ended by any means; nor is the end even in sight-and during the reconstruction period more will be expected of agriculture than of any other industry. Agriculture up to the present has met every demand made upon it and will continue to do so, but the most serious obstacle to the production programme which the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has asked the farmers of Canada to carry out is the man-power shortage, which demands immediate consideration and a prompt solution. The price problem also looms large. If the lack of man-power shackles the farmer, unsatisfactory prices must weaken his desire to produce. So, Mr. Speaker, this is a very serious problem.
In this connection the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) referred to an order in council passed recently, P.C. 246. Hon. members will find his statement in Hansard of February 26. One would judge from that, that the Minister of Labour was going to follow the principle on which the Minister of Agriculture acted on March 23, a year ago, when by order in council he froze farm labour. The Minister of Labour is going along practically the same lines. I wish these two ministers would get together, because if the policy which the Minister of Labour enunciated the other day is not carried out any better than was the order in council of the Minister of Agriculture last year, we shall continue in the same mess we are in to-day.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The farmer is working under serious difficulties. To no class has the war brought more production problems than it has to the farmer. At the present time, as we all know, he can get scarcely any new machinery. Even repairs are difficult' to get. This may be on account of war production. Shortages of labour, gasoline and tires are some of his headaches. He cannot compete in the matter of wages with war industry. So I say there are many problems brought about by the war with which the
farmer is confronted. Some hold that his difficulties would be solved by an increase in the price of farm products; but the situation to-day is such that the farmer does not know whether he will be able to continue in business.
Let me at this point make a brief comparison between the position of the Canadian farmer and that of his cousin across the line. I recently brought to the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) the fact that when the quota restrictions over there were lifted, wheat went to SI .50 and oats to the highest price in eighteen years. In the last three weeks under their new regulations they sold a hundred million bushels of wheat. The farmers over there have a storage allowance of one cent per bushel per month for seven months for grain stored on their farm, and advances have been made to them in respect of the grain stored there. What have we in Canada? Our farmers are still under the quota restrictions: wheat remains at 90 cents, and for oats 51i cents is the limit. There is no farm storage allowance, and no advance against grain within the quota still undelivered, on the farm. This is not fair to our farmers.' What has brought about the increase of price in the United States? In three days the United States houses and mill3 bought fifteen and a half million bushels of wheat on the Winnipeg market. The situation was so serious that the minister called an emergency meeting of the Canadian wheat board,-one of whose members, I regret to say, passed away on Friday last. I should like the minister to make a statement as to what is to be done. What are the circumstances under which the Americans are buying this wheat? Why is it going over there?
I come now to the debt burden of the western farmer. Under our quota delivery system, the creditor, whether a loan company or any land owner who has leased land to a tenant, gets one-third of the crop delivered under the quota; I refer to the undeliverable portion of one-third of the crop which is grown on the farm. But the loan company should not be allowed to charge the farmer interest on the amount or value of the undelivered portion. He would deliver it if he could; and I hope this grievance will be rectified as a result of the conference which is now being held in Ottawa. I hope too that the conference will result in some arrangement respecting the handling of farm debts in the west. I suggest, without going into detail regarding the situation in each of the prairie provinces, that a permanent board of review be established with power to adjust, either up or down, the payments which any
The Budget-Mr. Perley

farmer has to make in a given year. I would give the board blanket power to cover the province-I speak now particularly of Saskatchewan-in any one year to meet circumstances such as a general crop failure, and I would recommend that their rulings apply to all farmers, not to individuals, as they generally do.
Another suggestion I would make with respect to debt adjustment is this. For years I have consistently urged in this house that if the government had written off the debt arising from soldier settlement in respect of the last war, the country would have saved money. I advocate that as part of the proposed debt adjustment the soldier settlers' debts be written off. I have a letter from one district in which, of the twelve original soldier settlers, only one remains, and he is making a great effort [DOT] to carry on. After all, this concession would do no more than repay these men in some small measure for what they are doing in the present war. Their sons were the first to enlist and their daughters have followed-they are in the army too. Many of these settlers have left the farms to join the reserve forces or are members of the home guard. Their wives are carrying on with Red Cross work, preparing parcels for overseas, and engaging in other war activities in their districts. After all, the amount of the writeoff would be comparatively small.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is one of the things which would remain to be considered-what we should do for the others.
Let me now refer briefly to the matter of parity prices. I believe this principle should be adopted at once. The hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) and I introduced a resolution two years ago calling for the enactment of this principle, and I have now on the order paper a resolution on the subject. I believe farm prices, particularly the prices of grains, should be adjusted in relation to the farmer's costs of production. I will not read my resolution, because time is short, but will simply say that because of the important part which wheat plays in our national economy, there should be taken into consideration the setting of an initial price of SI. 10, as a step towards a parity price. I would then set the domestic price at SI .25, and I would pay storage for grain remaining on the farm which comes within the quota; also I would make an advance on grain still on the farm coming within the balance of the deliverable quota, up to seventy-five per cent of its value. That has been my stand for years.

In 1938 I moved in this house a resolution calling for a thorough consideration of prices from the long-term point of view, and suggesting one dollar for wheat. I was right, and those in authority are beginning to see it now. It is a matter of satisfaction to me that the federation of agriculture has approved the figure of one dollar, with SI .35 for wheat required for domestic consumption, and has made representations accordingly to the government. The pools ask for that. The grain men go a little further. I contend that so far as the domestic price is concerned there is no sound argument against it. We have the principle adopted to a certain extent in the processing tax. It has to come.
In a copy I have before me of the Leader Post, reference is made to the Votes and Proceedings of the Saskatchewan legislature, and to the fact that a Liberal member there, Mr. Danielson, moved in the house a resolution of which this is part.
That it is essential to the economic welfare of Saskatchewan that production of wheat be recognized as our major source of income and that the federal government be urged to accept through the Canadian Wheat Board no less than 280 million bushels of wheat at parity prices with an initial advance of not less than $1 a bushel.
It is with some satisfaction I see these men catching up, but they are several years late. I hope the Minister of Agriculture and the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) and other wmstern men will support my resolution when it comes up. They are closer to the government than I am and may be able to convince the cabinet. I know what some will say when we take up this resolution. The hon. member for Moose Jaw will say, what are you going to do with the surplus? I venture to say that before this debate closes there will be many pages of Hansard setting out figures with respect to our crop production and surpluses, how they have disappeared in other years, how they may disappear now. These figures are so much ejmwash. The principle of parity prices is there and this surplus need not cause any worry. I am not a pessimist. If the war ended to-morrow this surplus would disappear inside of six months. If the war ends next year the surplus may prove a blessing, because it will be needed to feed nations who are fighting beside us. I am not worrying about the surplus.
Another important matter, that of reconstruction, has been pretty well discussed, so that I shall not go into it now.
As to social security, the best form of it is an opportunity to rvork and an incentive to save, so that people may make sure of their

The Budget-Mr. Perley
own security. When the men come back from the war we shall have to be ready to give them employment, to reestablish them. Many of them were high school students or graduates of universities who never had a job. When they come back our economic system must be so managed that we can provide them with food, clothing and work. There must be no lapse of time between their discharge and their finding full employment at reasonable remuneration. Here again much will be expected of agriculture; it is one industry that can do much in absorbing these men. Many of the men will go back to their farms and take up farming as their life work. When we realize the contribution the farm makes every year to the national income it is something worth considering. Having regard to what has been done during the last two or three years in meeting the demands for increased production of animal products and other forms of food, and the contribution to the national income that the farmers have made, it is regrettable that they receive only about fifteen per cent of it in return.
I have a suggestion to make to meet this reconstruction period. It is that a thorough survey be made in Saskatchewan as to the possibilities of improving agriculture and farm as well as urban homes. The adoption or application of the housing scheme might be considered, as well as the question of power equipment for the farm home. Why should not every farm home, wherever it is possible, have electric light, refrigeration, and conveniences of the kind? There is also the possibility of developing power from our rivers and coal fields, as referred to by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) in this house on many occasions. Such a survey could do much towards providing employment for these men when they come back. There is the development of our oil fields and tar sands. I venture to say that in five minutes I could name five men as a board to make such a survey, and they could put 200.000 men to work in two months after the war in that province. These would be practical men who would do a job. The farms could easily absorb 100,000 men. I could mention also reforestation and roadbuilding. It appears to me that the government is not very anxious to have some of our natural resources developed as they should be, some of our products processed as they should be. The other day I asked the Minister of Agriculture if he had received a report from a Mr. Roston, who was head of a large power alcohol plant in eastern Europe, with respect to the utilization of agricultural products in
Canada. He said he had had a conversation with him and in a certain roundabout way had a report on this work from a Mr. Monahan. That report evidently might be of . value to us.
I have in my hand a clipping from the Chicago Tribune of February 13, 1943, reporting a statement made by one William J. Hale, of Minneapolis, who is research consultant for the Dow Chemical Company, of Midland, Michigan. He charges that an unpublicized reciprocal trade treaty had been made with South American nations providing for the destruction of all United States synthetic rubber plants after the war, which was the real reason for the reluctance of many companies to start rubber production. He went on to say:
We have signed an agreement in South America saying all plants built to make synthetic rubber will be wrecked after the war. . . .
He said that the rubber industry's birthright had been signed away. I am not going to read it all, but it is an interesting article. If such a thing is going on, does this government know anything about it? Does this government know of any agreement to destroy these synthetic rubber plants? Has it had any part in such agreements? I should like them to answer some of the questions put on the order paper with respect to the synthetic rubber plant that is proposed to be built at Sarnia. Under what conditions is that plant to be built?' Is it receiving any government assistance, and do they know anything about this agreement I have just mentioned?
Now I come to the income tax as it applies to the farmer. During the course of his address the minister said the farmer's tax had been eased in that it was proposed to enable a loss to be carried forward two years, so that if a farmer suffered a loss in 1942 he could charge it against the 1943 or 1944 tax. This is a step forward, and I commend the minister for having taken it, but I suggest that he is a little late, since last year that concession was given other businesses but was not extended to agriculture. In a return tabled not long ago it was stated that only 1,488 farmers in Canada had paid income tax last year, to an amount of $150,000 or an average of practically $100 each. There are 750,000 farmers in Canada, of whom approximately 150,000 are in Saskatchewan. I am going to offer a suggestion with respect to these farm incomes, because the tax collected really does not make it worth while bothering 750,000 farmers. I am going to suggest that the farmer, especially the farmer of western Canada, be allowed tq charge as part of his operating cost a fair
The Budget-Mr. Perley

wage paid to his wife and daughters and young sons who help him on the farm. I am going to go even further. If the minister will not consider taking that action, I am going to ask that every farmer in Canada be given exemption from the payment of income tax unless he can show $2,000 of a net income. These are two points I should like the government to take into consideration. I have received many letters asking me to bring them forward. Why should not the farmer be exempt? Industry is working on a cost plus basis; and compare the lot of the farmer with that of the salaried civil servant here in Ottawa. Why should not the farmer be exempt up to $2,000? I would remind the house that in many cases industries are writing off their capital investments in three years, and I believe the farmer should be given greater consideration along this line than he is receiving at present.
I come now to a matter which has been mentioned already in the house, the question of taxing cooperative dividend payments, or what are called patronage dividends. I trust the government will not consider imposing a tax upon the cooperatives of western Canada. The attitude of the Saskatchewan pool, which is the largest cooperative organization in the west, is that these dividends should not be taxed until they have been distributed to the individuals, who then would have to consider them as part of their income. I could place on record the position taken by the representatives of the pools in this con-, nection, but without doing that I trust the government will not consider the imposition of a tax of this kind.
Only a very small percentage of the revenue that will be raised through taxation will be returned to the farmer. The Minister of Agriculture has even reduced his estimates this year, and in some particulars I agree that this should be done. On the other hand, however, we had the announcement the other day of the setting up of a subsidies board, and it will be recalled that I asked the minister about this matter when it was first mentioned in the press, before he made his statement to the house. In the light of the statement of the Minister of Finance, however, in which it was estimated that nearly $60,000,000 will go to the producers this year, I venture to say that if they took only half that amount and added it to the price of grain in Canada, which on a 280,000,000 bushel quota would mean 10 cents a bushel, that would do more for agriculture generally than all the subsidies you could think of, having in mind all the boards and machinery that will have to be set up to carry out the administration of those

subsidies. When the Minister of Agriculture provides for more boards to operate in western Canada, with priority on gasoline, tires and so on, it looks to me like an election year, and we think we know what we will be seeing out there this summer.
I should like to refer briefly to the subamendment, which asks that old age pensions be increased, that our banks be nationalized, and so on. I take off my hat to no hon. member of this house in my advocacy of adequate pensions for the old, for widows and for the dependents of soldiers now in the armed forces. I have been consistent in my attitude in this regard, and I still support these pensions. I might not vote for the subamendment, because it involves other matters as well, but in any case I have made my position clear on that point.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, all I am pleading for is a fair deal to agriculture, particularly in the prairie provinces. I hope the government will take some action in regard to the man-power mess that now confronts us. During the short time I have been speaking I have advanced seven constructive suggestions: (1) an increase in the price of wheat to bring it more nearly to parity level; (2) a domestic price; (3) a permanent board to review the debt of the province of Saskatchewan each year, with blanket authority to deal with the matter; (4) farmers to be allowed to charge to the cost of operation a wage allowance for their wives and daughters and young sons; (5) exemption of the farmer from the income tax; (6) the debt of soldier settlers to be written off; (7) bonuses and subsidies and boards to be discontinued and half the amounts set aside in the estimates for such purposes to be added to the price of our farm commodities. One or two of these suggestions are new, and I hope they will receive consideration. I could take some considerable time to deal with matters such as price spreads, and so on, but they have been dealt with already this year.
Let me say in closing that no matter what may be our political differences we should now get down to work and devote every possible effort to the winning of this war. Let us do everything we can to see to it that when the time comes our men fighting on land and sea and in the air will be reinforced by trained men, fully equipped and properly fed and" clothed, so that in years to come we may have no regrets in connection with what we did in the year 1943. And may we be proud of the fact that we have placed Canada in the forefront of the united nations and of the empire, a place where it truly belongs.

The Budget-Mr. Mcllraith

maintopic: TAXING OF POOLS-STATEMENT OF MR. SPEAKER AS TO QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset may I pay tribute to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) for the budget he has brought down, both as to its content and as to its method of presentation. Canada is indeed fortunate in having the present minister in charge of its finances during this time of stress. Financial measures are now such that we have a very large section of our population in the taxpaying class. There has been a great extension in this field.
Very little has been said in the debate about the commendable attitude of these taxpayers in meeting their obligations, as they have done in the last two years. I should like also to say a word of appreciation of the voluntary organizations, and the churches of all denominations, which have done so much war work and have done it so well. It seems to me that so many have done so much work in this time with so little expression of appreciation from any source.
I should like to draw the attention of the house to some matters concerning the administrative arm of the government. In recent years the trend has been for that administrative arm to become more and more important, and this trend has been accelerated since the outbreak of war. To-day the Canadian government is the largest employer in Canada. The civil service generally has done a magnificent piece of war work. It is interesting to note that we do not hear anything about absenteeism when we discuss this class of war workers. There are, however, some matters concerning them which I feel should receive immediate attention and correction. The act setting up the civil service commission comes directly under the supervision of the Secretary of State (Mr. McLarty), and he is responsible for its administration. But his authority over the civil service generally seems to stop there, and we have a situation wherein the public service generally is not directly under the control of any minister of the crown.
Under the guise of controlling expenditures, the treasury board has gradually and continuously extended its authority over the personnel of the civil service, and has done this without giving the civil service any right of appeal, either to the treasury board or from its decisions. From time to time the Minister of Finance has dealt with matters affecting employer-employee relations in the public service. His responsibilities in this connection however are not clear. At the present time I believe we have the most competent minister of finance we have had since confederation; and yet, with due deference to him, I suggest
he ought not to be expected to deal with administrative matters affecting the civil service generally. They ought more properly to be dealt with by one of the other ministers who is not carrying the direct responsibility of a war portfolio. Either the authority of the Secretary of State should be clarified and enlarged, or that authority should be given to some other minister of the crown.
I have always held the view that the relationship between the dominion government as an employer and the civil sendee as a group of employees should serve as a model in labour or employer-employee relations for the country at large. In many respects long strides have been taken in the public service. In 1908 we had the adoption of the competitive system of appointments and promotions. That met with considerable opposition at the time of its adoption, and indeed at the present time there is still some little opposition to it. In 1924 we had the adoption of the present Civil Service Superannuation Act, which is probably the greatest boon ever given the public service in Canada. These two measures are indeed worthy of a model relationship. In some other respects, however, we have not gone forward. We are now at a point where there is some danger of these advances being to a very great extent nullified-nullified by the extension of treasury board control over the individual personnel of the service. It seems to me that this control by the treasury board is indirect control without direct responsibility.
There are many matters I could mention in this relationship as requiring attention. For purposes of illustration I shall deal only with four of them. I choose these four, not necessarily because they are the most important, but because perhaps they will better illustrate my point. The first matter has to do with what is known as the permanent-temporary quota system. Normally any person appointed by the civil service commission to a permanent position is given permanent appointment after serving a probationary period. The first serious interruption in this procedure came in 1932, when, by an order in council supplemented by a treasury board minute, the appointment of permanent employees was arbitrarily prevented, notwithstanding the nature of the work being done. That condition continued until July, 1935, when the ban on permanency was lifted.
The consequences of keeping an employee in a temporary category are grave. Apart from certain dislocations which must take place in the service there are two main consequences affecting such employee. One is
The Budget-Mr. Mcllraith

.that he cannot compete for promotion. He may have served many years in a temporary category; he may be the best employee for a certain kind of work, but notwithstanding these facts he is ineligible for promotion to the senior position next above the one he holds, in the event of its becoming vacant. The permanent employee, who may be doing inferior work, gets the promotion. In addition the temporary employee has not the right to contribute to the superannuation fund.
There are certain other inequalities affecting an employee who may be kept in a temporary category although doing permanent work. One of these is that he is not eligible for statutory increases. The unfairness and the dislocations can easily be seen.
After the lifting of the ban on permanency in 1935 the former condition was restored for some months. Then in 1936 the good wrork was undone by order in council 84978, and the temporary-permanent quota system was reestablished on a twenty per cent temporary basis.

speechtext:
I cannot give my hon. friend the number at the moment. The order in council was not quite as serious as the . order in council of 1932, but it embodied most of its fundamental faults, and it was the subject of continued and strong protests. In 1939 a committee of the House of Commons was set up under the chairmanship of the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) to inquire into the administration of the Civil Service Act generally. Representations were made to that body, and as a result in 1939 the committee on the Civil Service Act recommended that the temporary-permanent quota system be done away with. The report of the committee will be found in Votes and Proceedings of the House of Commons of Thursday, April 27, 1939. Paragraph 18 of the report reads as follows:
18. Your committee is of the opinion that:
(1) a departmental division of eighty per cent permanent and twenty per cent temporary results in discrimination in certain branches where the work is entirely permanent and -where twenty per cent have to wait years for any hope of permanency; and

(2) disapproves of any practice which will result in a branch creating work to bring in extra temporaries so as to absorb into the permanent quota those who otherwise would not be permanent.
As a result of that recommendation of the committee the ban on permanency was again lifted in 1939. There was again, general satisfaction throughout the service, but it was very short-lived. In May, 1940, the treasury board, by a minute of that body, established the quota system on a somewhat different basis but with all the primary faults of the old system. A percentage was established for each unit of the service on the basis of the total staff as of September, 1939. These percentages varied with the different units. It will be noticed that this is an absolutely rigid and arbitrary system and does not provide for any changing conditions in the departments. Under this system* we now have many employees working in the public service for many years in positions of a permanent character. These employees have no right to contribute to the superannuation fund, nor do they receive superannuation benefits. They have no right to compete for promotions in their own branches to positions immediately above the ones they hold. Not only is an injustice done- to the individuals concerned, but the public service suffers. These groups of employees are fairly well distributed across the country. The committee of the House of Commons dealt with this matter and made a recommendation thereon. Notwithstanding the fact that the government at that time saw fit to act on that recommendation, the treasury board reimposed this system upon the public service.
The second illustration I want to give has to do with prevailing rates employees and their exclusion from the benefits of the superannuation fund. The superannuation act has been in force since 1924, but a very large group of the public service of Canada are excluded from its benefits notwithstanding the fact that they may have worked in the public service for many years. The best example of this class of employee is to be found in the printing bureau at Ottawa. Many of the employees in the printing bureau have worked continuously for more than thirty years in the public service of Canada, yet they have no right to contribute to the superannuation fund, nor have they any right to receive the benefits from the superannuation or the retirement funds. We had an example last year of one man who had worked more than fifty years at the time of his retirement, but he was simply out, that was all.

He was a prevailing rates man. This term is used in connection with employees paid on a certain basis, but it is somewhat misleading. To go into all the incidence of it would probably extend my remarks beyond my time. They are those who are paid on a basis other than an annual stated salary. They are paid on an hourly basis at the printing bureau but they do not receive overtime on the usual prevailing rates basis. The main point is that their salary is other than a stated annual salary.
A committee of the House of Commons was set up to deal with this situation in 1938, and it heard evidence during that year and again during the session of 1939. This committee made its final: report to the House of Commons on May 5, 1939, in which it recommended that the prevailing rates employees should be eligible under the superannuation act. This recommendation is contained in paragraph 8, which reads:
That provision be made in the statute to render prevailing rates employees eligible to become contributors subject to designation by governor in council on the recommendation of the treasury board of the various classes and individuals to be so rendered eligible.
Notwithstanding this recommendation, nothing has been done to extend the benefits of the superannuation act to this class of employee.
The third point I desire to make is that no holidays are given to certain prevailing rates men.	In 1925, by order in council
P.C. 1936, prevailing rates employees were granted one week's holidays with pay in each year, subject to certain conditions and limitations. Most of the prevailing rates men in the service have been brought under that ruling at one time or another since 1925, but in 1941 it was discovered that a group of these men in the mines and geology branch of the Department of Mines and Resources did not have this right. I took the matter up with the Minister of Mines and Resources and it was corrected. It was thought at the time that all employees in the department were covered, but in 1942 it was discovered that a small number in the forest products laboratory had not been brought under the benefits of the order in council. The matter was taken up with the department but the treasury board ruled that they were not eligible to receive one week's holidays with pay. The number involved is not large, but many of these men have worked continuously for the department for more than fifteen years, yet the treasury board ruled that they were not eligible to receive these holidays with pay.
It is interesting to note two things in this connection. Apparently the treasury board had jurisdiction and was able to rule on the matter, although it did not directly concern the expenditure of public funds. The second point is that a comparatively small number was involved in this routine administration matter, and yet the minister of the department could not deal with it. He did not have the authority, yet the treasury board were able to have jurisdiction and to deal with it.
The fourth illustration concerns a small number of prevailing rates men who are not paid the prevailing rates established by the Department of Labour. The number of employees is small and the amount involved is small, yet because of its effect upon policy it is a matter of major importance. I refer particularly to some of the prevailing rates men working for the Department of Agriculture at the central experimental farm. There are two classes of carpenters working there, and I deal specifically with them because I am more familiar with their status. There are public works carpenters hired by the Department of Public Works who are working at the experimental farm and paid at the prevailing rate of wages. Then there are two or more departmental carpenters hired by the Department of Agriculture, working at the same place and paid a few cents an hour less.

I am glad the hon. member has gathered it. I mention only four of the problems that arise in the civil service but there are a great many others I could mention. There is the matter in the Department of Agriculture of the pay of certain technical staff doing research work, and their general reclassification. There is the question of statutory increases. There is question of the cost of living bonus for superannuated civil servants. But perhaps the four I have outlined will illustrate what I want to say, and the details of the other matters can be discussed on subsequent occasions.

The situation is that the treasury board is steadily and continually taking complete control of all matters affecting personnel in the government service, and this whether or not the direct expenditure of public money is involved. I am not aware that any government has at any time deliberately as a matter of policy decided that the treasury board should have this jurisdiction. The whole trend started in 1932. I am sorry to say that the then government was most ruthless and unfriendly towards the public service generally. That trend has not yet been checked, although many injustices have been removed.

speechtext:
It was restored in
modified form, and I am here protesting against it.
I have always held the view, Mr. Speaker, that we as members of the House of Commons are directly responsible for the expenditure of public funds, such is our traditional duty, and I feel perfectly sure that with the wide extension there has been in the number of taxpayers during the last few years we are going to be held answerable on that score. I do not think we should be under any illusions about it. Yet the present position is that in the House of Commons no minister is directly answerable as such for the administration of the public service.
The treasury board as a matter of practice has an enormous number of items coming before it for attention. As I said previously, I have never been able to get as full information as I desired about its workings, but I think it is reasonable to assume that the larger items receive the attention of the treasury board proper, while the smaller items, affecting small groups of personnel or individuals, are left to the staff of the treasury board. As

The Budget-Mr. Mcllraith
nearly as I can find out, and judging from the letters and documents that are signed, it seems to be the practice for the assistant deputy minister of finance to deal with these matters for the secretary of the treasury board.
Having regard to all the problems which have arisen, and other difficulties with respect to demobilizing some of the temporary staffs in the war departments, an advisory committee was set up in January of this year. It consists of five members. The chairman is Mr. Coon, an executive at the head office of the Bank of Nova Scotia. The secretary is the assistant deputy minister of finance, of whom I have just spoken. Another member is Mr. B. J. Roberts of the National Harbours Board, formerly assistant deputy minister of finance -the position now held by the secretary of the civil service committee-and the other two members are civil service commissioners. This committee is set up to advise the treasury board on matters affecting the civil service. Mr. Ronson, the assistant deputy minister of finance who is secretary of the advisory board, is to advise himself. Just how that process goes on I do not know; it is worthy of Gilbert and Sullivan at their best. I know very little about Mr. Coon, the chairman of the board, but I hope that the relationship between the banks and their employees is not to be the model for the relationship between the dominion government and its employees.
There is in Saturday's Ottawa Journal a report of an interview with Mr. Coon. I will read part of it:
For bankers, he-
That is, Mr. Coon.
-told the Journal this morning, spend their lives handling the "human element."
Where, he wanted to know, did a man take down his hair and talk over his problems, if he didn't do it when going to his bank manager for a loan?
The "human element" which now confronted him comprised some 40,000 civil servants demanding compensation for what they claim have been long-standing injustices, and on the other side, the treasury board standing guard over the government payroll.
The "human element" of this problem, he believed, was no tougher to tackle than that which he has been handling through the years as a banker.
I do not think this requires much comment. Although I do not know the relationship between bankers and persons seeking loans, I had not thought that the human element was particularly emphasized; I supposed that they used strict business methods. Nor do I suppose that persons seeking loans of bankers constitute such a wide section of the community, at that. In any event he is the chairman of the advisory committee, and I
have referred to the second and third members. As regards the two members who are civil service commissioners, I have nothing but the very highest praise for their work. Undoubtedly they would be the first witnesses called before any committee dealing with this matter.
The civil service generally has no confidence in the committee. I should have thought that a condition precedent to setting up any committee to deal with employer-employee relations would be that the parties concerned should have confidence in the committee. This is achieved usually in two ways. One is to appoint representatives of the employer on the one hand and of the employees on the other, and to have the chairman chosen by these two groups of representatives. That was not done in this case. The employees have no representation on the committee. Another method is to appoint an entirely independent committee, but that was not done in this case either. The complaint that the committee is not independent is, I believe, well founded, because the main representative, the secretary, is the person in the treasury board who deals with the matters out of which most of these complaints arise. A third method open in this case is a committee of the House of Commons. Such a committee could properly have been set up here, because the House of Commons after all is responsible for the administration of the public business and for the expenditure of the public funds. This method might well have been used in the present instance; it has been used in the past, and I have referred to some of the rulings of such a committee.
One thing I wish to say just before closing. In regard to the two members of the advisory committee to whom I have particularly referred, I want to make it perfectly clear that I am not discussing their records as public servants. I am well aware that civil servants in general have no method of replying when anything is said about them in the House of Commons. I appreciate that fact, and I am not in any way attacking these gentlemen as public servants; so far as I know their records as such are quite good. What I am attacking is their fitness to function on this particular committee. I believe that should be made clear; otherwise my remarks might easily be misconstrued.
I have taken some time to go into this matter of the administrative arm of the government service. I have done so because I fear what is taking place will work injustice to the individual employees concerned and also be-
The Budget-Mr. Mcllraith

cause the trend in this connection is important and significant. Originally after confederation appointments to the public service were made in a quite haphazard manner, and I fear, in many instances, without much examination as to the fitness and qualifications of the prospective employee for the work to which he was to be assigned. In 1908 was instituted the merit system of appointments and promotions. That was opposed at the time, but the opposition is gradually dying out and the system in general is well established throughout the service. In 1924 a very fine superannuation act was set up, and it has since been extended. All these progressive measures, all the improvements made over a period of some thirty-four years, are now in danger of being nullified by this insidious extension of authority of the treasury board over the personnel of the public service. This is an extension without the treasury board having been directly and immediately given authority over the personnel of the public service as such. It is an extension in a form which does not charge any minister of the crown with direct responsibility as such so that he may be answerable to us here in the House of Commons.
It is for these reasons, Mr. Speaker, that I have taken the time of this honourable house to-day to bring these matters forward.

speechtext:
Fortunately or unfortunately I do not write my speeches, so that I am unable to do that. The hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. MacKenzie) the other night proposed that speeches here should be limited to twenty minutes instead of forty. I think the house will readily understand that the hon. gentleman is on the government side so that he perhaps feels that everything is as it should be. But some of us in the opposition do not feel that way about it, and therefore believe that we are entitled to at

least forty minutes to place before this house the views of those who are oppressed and to seek remedies for their troubles.
The budget address was one o.f the best I have' heard here so far as delivery is concerned, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) has been complimented from all parts of the house. I can extend my compliments to him as far as the presentation is concerned, but I think condemnation would come from certain classes by reason) of certain things that are in the budget. I believe the minister is doing his best; he has a big job, and I am blaming to some extent his advisers and the system under which he is working for some of the wrongs contained in this budget. Before going further I wish to express an opinion which may or may not meet with the approval of the house, but it looks to me that there is an election pending. Not long ago the Minister of Finance went on the air, on a Sunday evening I believe, and announced a reduction in the price of tea, coffee, oranges and milk. We are now promised something in connection with tariffs. I will read the part to which I have reference, as reported at page 861 and 862 of Hansard:
The government has already, by an exchange of notes with the United States on November 30 last, undertaken to enter into conversations with that country, and with other countries, for the purpose of formulating programmes of agreed action direction toward the expansion, after the war, of production, employment and the exchange and consumption of goods, to the elimination of all forms of discriminatory treatment in international commerce and to the reduction of tariffs and other trade barriers.
Committed to these objects and having in mind particularly the vital concern of this country in access to the selling and buying markets of the world, the government is prepared to discuss with the government of the United States, the government of the United Kingdom, or the governments of other countries with which we trade, reciprocal trade arrangements wdder in scope and longer in duration than have hitherto been made, provided always that the advantages of such arrangements shall be open to other countries willing to adhere to the same terms.
I am wondering whether that is just a little bait. If a thing is good for this country, there is no poorer excuse for not putting it into effect than that there is a war on. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has told us on different occasions that reform must come, and if it is not brought about before the war is over, it will be too late. I realize as do all hon. members, that at the present time we are having better terms with the United States than we have had for some time past, and after the war is over perhaps

The Budget-Mr. Fair
we shall have difficulty in establishing trade relations with the United States which could be very easily obtained at this time.
I do not find any provision made in the budget for bringing up to parity the price of wheat. Perhaps before dealing with that question I might go back to tariffs, because I see the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) in his seat and because of what have been termed hand-outs to farmers of the west, particularly in the way of bonuses and acreage reduction payments, I wish to show that western farmers have been getting back during the past few years just a trickle of what has been taken from them in the past by way of tariffs as one instance.
The late Hon. Norman Rogers made a survey in 1931 which is the last survey that has been made as far as I know. That survey showed that Manitoba in that year paid by way of tariffs $29,185,740, equivalent to $13.25 for every man, woman and child in that province. The corresponding figures for the other western provinces were:
