maintopic: TAXING OF POOLS-STATEMENT OF MR. SPEAKER AS TO QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It looks as if the people of Ontario have milked Alberta dry so that Alberta was not able to pay the interest, and rather than pay it the government of Alberta had the good sense to see that they kept their people alive. I commend them for doing so. Give the people of Alberta a square deal and 72537-79
they will pay their interest. Furthermore, if they had had a square deal it would not be necessary for them to borrow all that money so that the interest would not pile up.
I said I sympathized with the hon. member who spoke just before me. Some time last month we find that the wartime prices and trade board passed an order giving restaurant keepers a right to increase the price of tea and coffee served with meals by five cents; that is, ten cents for tea, coffee or milk served with meals. They are also allowed to charge ten cents if a person sits down at a lunch counter and has a drink of tea, coffee or milk. On February 22 I placed some questions on the order paper in this connection; they were made an order for return and as yet I have not received the information; but as far as I can see, the restaurants were not justified in demanding this increased price, if they did demand it. Some say they did, while we find that other restaurants have not increased their prices. It seems to me that those who have increased their charges could very well get along without that increase, because I do not believe the restaurants of Canada ever had as much business as at the present time. Usually increased business tends to decrease the overhead, and I believe that is so in the restaurant business as well. In addition, we find that the servings have been very considerably cut down. When you get a serving of meat or fish, in many cases you do not get more than one-third the serving you got before the war; and when it comes to sugar with which to sweeten your tea or coffee, you find that the lump has been sliced in three. You are given three of those slices, which means you receive the equivalent of one lump.
In addition, I believe these restaurants are saving a little in connection with dish washing. Some of them are so rushed that they cannot keep their dishes properly washed. I was in a restaurant in this city not long ago when I saw five cups being given to five customers without the cups having been washed. One of the customers drew the attention of the waitress to the marks on the side of the cup where the other person had drunk the coffee. The waitress took a paper napkin, held it under a hot-water tap, went around, wiped off the cup and placed it before the customer. That customer had only about five minutes in which to get back to work, so that he had to go ahead and drink from a cup that had not been washed. This is not good enough. The people who go to the Chateau Laurier or some of the better restaurants do not get that

The Budget-Mr. Fair

sort of service; but the people who imposed this tax do not eat in the small restaurants of this or any other city in Canada.
Now we come to the low salaried workers, for instance the group who have $660 left after paying their income tax, of whom we have some thousands right in this city. My information is that it costs these people an average of $20 a month for a room, or $240 a year. Then I believe they are entitled to $1 a day for food, figuring 25 cents for breakfast, 35 cents for lunch and 40 cents for dinner. Certainly they will not overeat at that rate. This amounts to another $365, and when you consider the extra 15 cents a day that is charged by a number of restaurants in connection with beverages, you have another $54.75 tacked on to the living expenses of those compelled to eat in restaurants. That gives you a total of $659.75, which leaves a worker in this group with 25 cents with which to buy clothing and other necessities, soap, towels and all that sort of thing. Then people in this group are also asked to buy war bonds, war savings certificates and stamps; to help the Red Cross, the aid to Russia fund, the milk for Britain fund, the Chinese relief fund, and all the other funds that call upon the public for contributions. During the past two or three weeks I have had in this connection a number of letters, of which I am going to read two. One is from the city of Montreal; the other is from the city of Vancouver, which will indicate that people all across the dominion are feeling the effects of this new tax. The first letter reads:
Dear Sir,
I trust you will pardon the liberty I have taken in addressing you.
I note your remarks re "coffee price boost" and that any person obliged to eat in restaurants would increase the cost of living by about $55 a year.
If you lived in Montreal and was obliged to limit the cost of your meals to 30 cents, as I have to do, it would increase your living costs to $76.65 a year.
All meals of 35 cents and over are taxed 5 per cent, which means your 30 cent meal would cost 37 cents, made up as follows: meal, 30; beverage, 5; tax, 2. The party responsible for this unnecessary increase should have his head examined.
That is signed by J. Anderson, of Montreal. The letter from Vancouver is as follows:
_ Your remarks regarding the recent increase in the restaurant prices of tea, coffee and milk used as a beverage made in the house yesterday and reported in this morning's Vancouver paper are very much to the point.
This agency, which deals chiefly with the problems of unattached men, the majority of whom are in the low income group, and who live in rooming houses and obtain their meals in [Mr. Fair.j
restaurants, has already found it necessary to give supplementary aid as a result of the higher cost of meals.
Of this group, the old age pensioners and recipients of war veterans allowances are particularly hard hit. The majority of these cases are unfit for employment and are unable to supplement their $25 a month income.
A rough breakdown of their living costs shows rent averaging $8 a month, miscellaneous items including clothing, laundry, soap, razor blades, car tickets, etc., $5, balance for food $12. On an average of a thirty day month this means that the man is required to purchase meals within a limit of 40 cents a day. The general practice is the purchase of two 20 cent meals. The five cents a meal increase for beverage amounts to $3 a month.
Unless some action is taken either to rescind the wartime prices and trade board order or to give a supplementary grant to recipients of old age pension and war veterans allowance, the already inadequate standard of living of these groups and other small pensioners, etc., will be considerably lowered.
I am wondering if the government or industry will pay a cost-of-living bonus to those who eat in restaurants, to recompense them for this inflationary rise in the cost of their meals. If that is not done I suggest now that labour see to it either that this bonus is paid or that the increase in the cost of these beverages is removed. There is no justification for it, in my view, and I should like to see something done.
If we listen to after-dinner speeches we will not believe that there are hard times anywhere in this country. I do not believe we can ever attain the golden age of economic life while we are living in the stone age of economic thought. We have to do much better than we have done in the past. On December 2 of last year the Prime Minister was in New York where he spoke to the Pilgrims of America. He is reported as having used these words:
The only path to prosperity and peace is the path of equality of cooperation and of human brotherhood. The new order must be a world order. It must be governed by a universal rule of law. It must be based on human rights and not on the right of property, privilege or position. An end must be put to monopoly of power by any country and by any class.
Again I remind the house that the Prime Minister has told us on many occasions that we must have reforms before the war is over; otherwise it will be too late. What are we doing about it? As I said at the commencement of my speech this afternoon, if something good can be put into effect, then the war would seem to be the poorest possible excuse for not taking action,
In Canada we have a problem respecting people who are not able to supply themselves with medical and hospital accommodation.

The Budget-Mr. Fair
I am suggesting now to medical men in the house, and their friends outside the house who are well organized throughout the country, that they demand from this and from any other government which may be in office later, that free medical service and hospitalization be granted to all those unable to provide it for themselves. Prevention of ill-health would be the cheapest possible way of cutting down the number of heavy bills now being paid for these services.
Canada can produce sufficient to satisfy all the needs of our people, but apparently we are not able to produce enough for the human greed being practised. In respect of old age pensioners I do not think it is necessary for me to go into detail. Already several hon. members have brought the case affecting these pioneers to the attention of the house, and the letter I read in connection with the increase in the price of meals gives information respecting the distribution of the small amount they now receive. We continually receive letters from old age pensioners and potential old age pensioners asking that the age for the receipt of pension be lowered, and that the amount be increased to at least $30 a month, also that a pensioner be allowed a net annual income of 1500 a year instead of $365 as at present. This I believe would not be any hardship on the country. We could make adjustments which, would not injure anybody, but would greatly help these old people. Pensions paid other people, such as persons in other parts of this building, might very well be used along this line.
Then we must give consideration to veterans of the great war of 1914-18. A number of these men need assistance, and I am speaking particularly for the veterans who settled under the Soldier Settlement Act. I believe I stated their case fairly thoroughly and in some detail on February 3 last, and I shall not go into it at length at this time. I intend, however, to return to it on another occasion, and I hope hon. members will get some information respecting these men and be prepared before the close of the session to obtain something worth while, reasonable and just for these settlers.
On November 19 of last year order in council No. 10472 was passed. We were told that this order in council would improve the lot of soldier settlers. Having read it, I feel that it is no more or less than a sentence of another twenty years to the hell these people have been enduring for the last twenty or twenty-five years. This is not good enough. As their representatives, let us see to it that something reasonable and just is done.
Looking back over the years I have been in the house, I think of the letters I have received and of the delegations of widows of veterans of the last war. Very little has been done for them up to the present time. However I see in the estimates an amount is provided to make provision for these people. I do not believe the amount is large enough.
We now come to the men and women returning from the present war. On another occasion I asked that they be given a square deal now, rather than twenty years after the war is over. In this connection I received a resolution from the Lloydminster branch, No. 39, of the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League. This resolution, dated March 10, is as follows:
Be it resolved that the Lloydminster Branch No. 39, Canadian Legion, B.E.S.L. records its protest against the inadequacy of the maintenance and unemployment benefits of $9 per week for single men, and $13 per week for married men, as set forth in Acts and Orders in Council governing the rehabilitation of returned soldiers; that we condemn the limitations contained in those Acts and Orders in Council, and deplore the fact that reestablishment measures, so far, have been based upon the presumption of the existence of a set of post-war conditions which we feel should not be taken into consideration in the framing of an effective rehabilitation programme.
C. Bexson,
Secretary, Lloydminster Branch, Canadian Legion, B.E.S.L.
This question will be dealt with later on, and I trust that hon. members and particularly those who served overseas in the last war, will see to it that something worth while is done for those men, upon their return; and that preparation be made before the war is over, because, according to our Prime Minister, that will be too late.
I hold in my hand a clipping from the Saskatchewan Cooperative Consumer. I have used it before in the house, but I shall read it again because I believe it illustrates in a form better than I could offer the conditions now existing. It is headed with the word "Parable", and reads:
Count Leo Tolstoy has written a parable concerning the private profit system, which portrays in realistic fashion a state of affairs that is all too true.
I see mankind as a herd of cattle inside a fence enclosure. Outside the fence are green pastures and plenty for the cattle to eat, while inside the fence there is not quite enough grass for the cattle.
Consequently, the cattle are trampling underfoot what little grass there is and goring each other to death in their struggle for existence.
The Budget-Mr. Fair

I saw the owner of the herd come to them and when he saw their pitiable condition, he was filled with compassion for them and thought of all he could do to improve their condition.
So he called his friends together and asked them to assist him in cutting grass from outside the fence and throwing it over the fence to the cattle.
And that they called Charity.
Then because the calves were dying off and not growing up into serviceable cattle, he arranged that they should each have a pint of milk every morning for breakfast.
Because they were dying off in the cold nights, he put up well-drained and beautiful sheds for the cattle.
Because they were goring each other in the struggle for existence, he put corks on the horns of the cattle, so that the wounds they gave each other might not be serious.
Then he reserved a park in the enclosure for the old bulls and the old cows over 70 years of age.
In fact he did everything he could think of to improve the condition of the cattle, and when I asked him why he did not do the obvious thing, break down the fence and let the cattle out, he answered:
"If I let the cattle out I should no longer be able to milk them."
On behalf of those who are overseas fighting and those who are returning from the war and who in the future, if we do not take action, will be in the same class as those who are to-day old age pensioners, I would say that they are in the same category as and would compare with those referred to as cattle inside the fence. It is about time we broke down the fence and made available to these people the good things that this country can produce.
We have in this country an instrument that nullifies the rights of the elected representatives of the people. In another portion of this building is a body of men without any particular qualification except service to their political parties. These men under our present constitution have the right to nullify any act passed by the elected representatives of the people. We are told that many years ago the Liberal party tvere going to reform that particular house. We are told that there is a constitution which stands in our way, but as far as I am concerned that constitution is man-made and it can be man-changed and made to serve the people to-day rather than those interests which saw to it that when it Was drawn up it would serve their purpose.
Perhaps we are not prepared to make this change in our constitution because we have not a quill pen to do it with. I understand that when this document was drawn up years ago a quill pen was used, but to those who would put forth this kind of argument I would suggest that we have many geese and

turkeys running around our farmyards and it would be quite easy if it were thought necessary to take a quill from one of their wings to make the change. By doing this we would make available for other purposes thousands and thousands of dollars every year, and a number of offices now inhabited by people who are making no good use of them would be made available to others. We could stop appointing people to this house, and those who are there who can qualify for the old age pension could be granted $30 a month.
No reform can come to the common people unless the lawmakers are of the same mind as the common people. This may be a clumsy way of putting it, but I say that unless the common people get a majority of members in this house who are in actual sympathy with them, we cannot expect to have much change in favour of the common people. God must love the common people because he made so many of us. I have not much time left so that I shall have to hustle along a little faster than I intended.
We must have a firm foundation for our new set-up; other-wise it will crumble. In order to have this firm foundation, I suggest that there should be a better deal for agriculture. After all, agriculture is the basic industry of this country, the one that must stand the brunt of taxation, directly or indirectly, and the one that must provide the food for all of us in Canada, as well as many of the men who are being sent overseas to fight our battles. In order to give agriculture a square deal I suggest that there should be parity prices for all agricultural products.
We should have a long range programme so that the farmer can go ahead and make plans for a number of years instead of having to confine himself to a one-year programme. Farm debts have been accumulated under unjust legislation. When the prices of our products are forced down there is no talk of scaling down either interest rates or the debts themselves. The result is that our farmers are now in an impossible position and cannot hope to get on a sound footing until something is done along the line I suggest. I am suggesting that the wishes of the western debt conference which is meeting in Ottawa to-day be implemented and placed upon the statute books here because this government and the privy council claim that the provinces have not this power.
Tariffs should be removed. I think I gave enough figures this afternoon to convince anybody that an imposition has been placed on

The Budget-Mr. Gregory
the farmer in this connection. I have some rather interesting information here in connection with income taxes paid by farmers. Between 1930. and 1942 an average of 1,191 farmers paid income tax, the average amount a year being $92,163. Because our farmers work longer hours than any other group; because they are not allowed wages for their wives or members of their families who may help them, I suggest that the government would not be losing much money to exempt the farmers from income taxation. This may seem to be class discrimination, but I think I am justified in asking for it on account of the conditions under which our farmers have been compelled to live during years gone by. If exemption cannot be granted, I suggest that the term for computing income tax be five years rather than the two as suggested in the budget. Proper steps should be taken to care for our aged pioneers who are underprivileged through no fault of their own, as well as for the veterans and veterans' wives of the first great war and the veterans and their families of the present war.
There is one answer and key to this-social credit. Since coming here in 1935 we have been laughed at on different occasions. As suggested the other night by one of the hon. members in front of me, hollow laughter means idle brains or empty brains, if you want to call them that. We do not have so much of this laughing now, and I think in future more consideration will be given to our suggestions. Up to the present time social credit has not been implemented. Let me say in conclusion that it is better to fail temporarily in something that must inevitably come, than to succeed in something that must ultimately fail.

maintopic: TAXING OF POOLS-STATEMENT OF MR. SPEAKER AS TO QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish first to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) upon bringing down a budget for the Canadian people which has added very little burden to their shoulders, notwithstanding the fact that Canada's contribution to the united nations has increased enormously. I believe that the budget delivered at this session will go down in history as one of the great documents in the life of Canada. I believe further that the name of the Minister of Finance will find a niche in the halls of the celebrities of Canada. I can only wish the minister a growing distinction, an added stature and increased usefulness in the public life of Canada.
I was very much impressed by an article written by the United States newspaper commentator, Ernest Bindley. This was written for United States consumption and is in praise
of Canada's policy step by step in financing the war. He narrates these steps in controlling inflation, in establishing a price ceiling, in our payment of bonuses, in the refundable tax feature of the income tax and in the fact that the provinces were being reimbursed for vacating the fields of income tax, corporation tax and succession duties. He ends this notable article by saying:
The war tax programme of the Canadian government has revealed a firm grasp of the essentials of wise management of the war economy which our tax programme-
He is referring to that of the United States: -has lacked.
His concluding remark is:
Congress could profit by studying the Canadian budget messages.
I am sure that we as Canadians have reason to be highly gratified that we have been the forerunners, that we blazed the trail along these lines and that our great neighbours to the south of us are now following in our footsteps, at times rather haltingly, rather hesitantly, it may be, but nevertheless endeavouring to follow step by step the plan as set forth by the government of Canada.
When I last spoke in this house on February' 8, I was predicting a change in the fiscal policy of Canada after the war. I had made certain statements to the effect that we would all be free traders or at least believers in low tariffs after the war is over, and I had started to develop that argument, sir, when my time was exhausted. I wish first to-day to finish that argument.
I said on that occasion that in the primitive days of Canada's industrial growth the home market was the only market Canada had for her manufactured products. Thus a policy of protection of the home market by a high tariff was built up as a policy for the protection, of industry in Canada, and it has continued ever since the "national policy" of 1874 was first initiated.
As Canada's industries expanded, its surplus products looked for foreign markets. Thus arose our export trade. But the home market being the main market was still protected. This doctrine had its fullest practical scope during the Bennett regime of 1930-35.
We have, however, gone through an industrial revolution during the last two years. We have become a prodigy of industrial production. When peace returns and war orders cease, our factories must turn to peacetime production and there will be a feverish search for export trade to keep the factories
The Budget-Mr. Gregory

going, to continue the employment of those at present engaged in those factories and to create jobs for the soldiers returning home. The tables then will have completely reversed -the home market will be the insignificant market and the export market will be the important one. It seems to me that the whole psychology of the people of Canada will change when this is realized. The psychology of the producer and the consumer, of the farmer and the businessman, of the worker and the management-the psychology of the whole Canadian people will have gone through a radical change. They will realize two great urges which will induce a change of tariff policy in Canada. May I indicate those two urges.
Efficiency and cheapness of production will be the essentials in order that Canadian goods may compete in price and quality in the open competitive markets of the world. I submit that high tariff protection is not conducive either to efficiency of operation or to cheapness of production.
The second urge may be put in this way. Exports have to be paid for, and how are exports paid for? Well, sir, the farmers of western Canada have always understood that very simple problem in arithmetic. Exports must always be paid for by imports. Hence the western farmers' consistent belief in free trade or low tariffs to permit a two-way traffic in commodities. I repeat what I said the last time I addressed the house, that after the war there will be no crusted high tariff Tories, that after this war is over we shall all be free traders or low tariff believers. The farmers of western Canada will welcome that day. It will mean the striking off of their chains of economic slavery. Poverty has been enforced on the western farmer by the heavy toll of freight rates on what he sells and on what he buys, by the artificially high prices which protective tariffs have compelled him to pay, and by a banking system unsuited in its structure and in its practices to be of service to the farmers of western Canada. I shall have something further to say as I develop my speech with respect to another kind of financing of western Canada, both in its activities and in its policies.
Leaving the question of a change which we believe is imminent in the fiscal policy of Canada, may I lay down the second proposition which to me is equally important. Not only must there be, after this war is over, a free interchange of commodities for the prosperity of Canada and the welfare of Canadian people, but there must be a free exchange of people. In other words, we must go back
(Mr. Gregory.]
once more to an active, generous, comprehensive immigration policy for the Dominion of Canada, subject always, of course, to the application of certain approved standards of physical, mental and moral fitness of those who seek entry into this country. Just in passing, after forty-five years' residence in western Canada and having seen nearly all the immigration into western Canada, may I say that often in the past these standards of physical and mental and moral fitness were applied with most inexcusable laxity. I believe that vast groups of European people will be eager to come to Canada after the war, to leave behind them forever the regular periodical recurrences of invasion of their homes, the fleeing for their lives and abandoning of their possessions which has been the history of countless generations throughout the whole history of Europe. I wonder if we do not at times forget that the same hills and rivers which Julius Caesar fought for, the same hills and rivers which nations and tribes, before those nations, fought for throughout the ages of Europe, are the same hills and rivers which our soldiers fought for in the great war of 1914-1918 and which the German armies in this war seized in their conquest of Europe.
Canada will have an opportunity such as she has never had in the past of selecting and choosing, that is hand-picking, the kind of immigrant that she will accept after this war. This policy will not be, like past policies, agricultural, designed to fill up vacant lands, because all the good vacant lands in western Canada are already filled. It will be one of selecting skilled tradesmen, artisans, technicians and industrialists. Prior to the outbreak of this war the breaking-down of mass population and centralized industry had commenced. Indeed, the decentralization of industry and population was well on its way. The bombing plane has simply hastened this movement by destroying the physical assets of thousands of factories in Europe and ending the lives of tens of thousands of skilled artisans working therein. The urge to get away from this kind of thing, from this incessant scourge in Europe, will induce innumerable industrialists to pack up what remains of their plant and machinery, their assets, their currency, their finances and credit, bring with them their technicians and artisans, and cross the ocean to Canada and this great land mass of north America, where they can reestablish themselves on a smaller scale, and, if not entirely free from bombing planes, at least live on this new land mass of north America where no wars break out, and to

The Budget-Mr. Gregory
attack which, bombing planes first have to cross two thousand miles of the Atlantic ocean or seven thousand miles of the Pacific ocean.
I believe that very often we fail to realize how fortunate we are in living upon this great land mass of north America. It is God's gift to the unfortunates of this war. Canada can be the land of the second chance for those who have lost their first chance in Europe because of the devastation of this war. I believe, then, that Canada will have a wonderful opportunity to enrich its economic life through a vast stream of wealth and credit, of industrialists, technicians and artisans, and the creation of a new population based upon secondary industry. The opposition of farm groups and farm organizations in western Canada to further immigration, an opposition which has been so prominent for at least the last fifteen years, will vanish, and the dawn of a new day will break on the horizon for western Canada.
What will the establishment of secondary industry mean to western Canada? Let me enumerate the answers in the following manner:
First, it will mean an increased home market for the consumption of commodities grown on the farm. It will mean the bringing of millions of new mouths to the grain fields of western Canada to consume our flour, meat and dairy products. Also, ini time, it will mean the building up of a domestic price for flour, meats, dairy products and other farm produce; and the export price which now governs the price of western farm products, and which has been the economic curse of our farmers as long as I have known anything about the effect of markets upon our producers, will apply only to that small balance which is left over, which we will call the exportable surplus.
Second, it will mean employment for our boys and girls. I do not wish to enlarge upon one of the saddest stories with which we are afflicted in western Canada. In only the second generation of pioneers who went to the prairies-unlike Great Britain, which looked after succeeding generations, even to the tenth generation before its emigrants scattered over the world-our people have had to suffer the sorrow and ignominy of seeing their boys and girls, born in the west, growing up there, attending its schools, for the cost of which we were responsible, when they reached the age when they are bubbling over with enthusiasm and energy and the desire to do something in this world, look in vain for jobs in the country of their upbringing, and become compelled to go to other provinces and throughout the United States of America,
where by their efforts they are enriching the life of other provinces or another country at the expense of the province in which they were born.
In the third place, it will mean relief from the heavy burden of taxation which weighs upon the towns and cities of Canada.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When the house rose at six o'clock I was trying to answer the question which I had put to the house, "What will the establishment of secondary industry mean to western Canada?" I had come to the third effect in answering that question. I had said it will mean relief from the heavy burden of taxes in our towns and cities, due to the increased assessment of factories, houses, warehouses, stores and all the development incidental to turning western Canada into a province of secondary industry.
Fourth, it will mean the turning of deficits of our two railway systems into permanent surpluses. Fifth, it will mean a reduced burden in servicing our bonded indebtedness, federal, provincial and municipal, on account of the increased realty values which will result in our towns and cities and farm lands and 'by reason of the increased number of wage-earners, the reduction of the per capita debt automatically will mean the reduction of per capita taxation. And sixth, it will permit the extension of increased social services for the reasons which I have stated.
It must be borne in mind that Canada has built up an overhead structure capable of maintaining a population of 50,000,000 people, in her railways, schools, civic improvements, legal structures of all kinds, publicly owned equipment, and in our mercantile and financial institutions. The burden of this structure on 11,000,000 people has become almost intolerable.
Following this war, certain things must be done to ensure the proper development of Canada along these lines. This evening I intend to lay three stones as a foundation for greater prosperity, greater happiness and a growing population in our national life.
I take the first stone, and a prominent stone in that foundation, to be the creation under the Bank of Canada of regional banks for the four natural regions of Canada. In order that this may be very plain may I answer the question, What are those four natural regions? In my judgment they are the maritime provinces, the central provinces, the
The Budget-Mr. Gregory

prairie provinces, and British Columbia, all having natural resources and an economy all their own and a geographical position in accordance with the position which they must occupy in that national whole which we call the confederation of Canada. The creation, I say, under the Bank of Canada of regional banks for the four natural regions of Canada. For what purpose? To use the credit that can be created against the wealth in production of each of these regions. It will be done through subsidiaries of existing banks, setting up agricultural banks, long-term credit banks, by our present institutions or the setting up of a special agricultural bank structure under the Bank of Canada in each of those regions to encourage the development of new resources and industries based on those resources and the general balanced development of that region which it is its duty to advance.
I realize that in laying a foundation for a new Canada this immediately breaks up the present situation, whereby through the present banking set-up the credit of this dominion has been and is being used for the maintenance of the industrial and financial preponderance of the central provinces at the expense of the other provinces of the dominion. I do not need to explain this point; I have spoken fully concerning it in the past in connection with the unfortunate breaking down of the conferences having to do with the Sirois report. I do not intend to take time now to expand this point; I just say that in one short lifetime I have seen the obliteration of industrial and financial institutions and their subsidiaries, insurance and trust companies in the maritime provinces, either by absorption by or removal to the central provinces, or by bankruptcy. In one generation I have seen the prodigious wealth of the prairie provinces flow in irresistible tide to the central provinces, leaving those prairie provinces barren of wealth, sucked as dry as a squeezed lemon.
Surely, sir, this was not the design or pattern intended or anticipated by the fathers of confederation. Surely the fathers of confederation never visualized a lopsided development such as we have in Canada at present. Surely those famous fathers never intended to pour into any such lopsided mould from the melting pot of the four crown colonies comprised in confederation. I would rather think that the fathers of confederation conceived the idea of each part of the new Canada contributing to the welfare of each of the other parts, each contributing something to the common cause in making a greater, happier and more prosperous Dominion of Canada.

I believe the time has come to do something about this problem. We should start now and reshape this distorted growth that we call the Dominion of Canada.
The second stone to which I would refer as a foundation of a new and better Canada is the setting up of an economic board for each of those four regions to conduct a rigid research for raw products within that region and to aid in their manufacture.
Without dwelling on that point, I come to the third stone, setting up of regional research laboratories to conduct research into more varied use of the products and commodities native to each of those regions. Speaking of my own particular part of the country, I refer to such commodities as wheat, wild weeds, low grade coal, oil, gas, clays, and timber native to the region.
It may be said that it was the purpose of the Sirois report, if it had been implemented, so to equalize things in Canada that all these grievances to which I have referred would be remedied. It is true the Sirois report proposed the setting up of subsidies to the less favoured provinces in order to equalize the standards of living of all the provinces, to equalize educational opportunities and other standards in all the provinces, and to assist in the servicing of the provincial debt of these provinces. But even if we assume for a moment that all these things had been accomplished, there would still remain the hollow shell of economic deficiency in parts of Canada, in my part of the country, arising from lack of production, not primary but secondary. Eventually this will lead to economic discontent which may place a socialist or other non-demoeratic group in control in some of the provinces, and merely postpones the date of the internal disruption between the federal and provincial authorities.
Now, sir, I should like to mention, in addition to the three stones which in my judgment are essential as the foundation of a new and better Canada, certain aids to make this structure a success. I say, first, that we should begin now, particularly in the prairie provinces, to carry on the technical training of our youth in order to prepare them for the new day in secondary industry. You may say that the dominion-provincial youth training scheme is already in existence. That is quite true, and I am pleading simply for a continuation of that scheme following the termination of this war. Second, the time must come in western Canada when there must be more intensive farming to diversify and raise the value per acre of our crops and put more labour content into their production. Next I plead for a greater

The Budget-Mr. Gregory
application of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, to take unsuitable land out of cultivation, and put it into community pastures, and to conserve water at every opportunity. I plead with this house and this government that larger and still larger sums be voted under that rehabilitation act for the purpose of carrying on conservation work in western Canada.
This brings me to the question of irrigation, and for a moment I should like to refer to an irrigation project which has nothing whatever to do with the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. It so happens that near my home, in the valley of the Saskatchewan river, there is a thousand acres of pasture, scrub and alkali which in the early days of the northwest mounted police, when their headquarters were in Battleford, was used as a pasture for the horses. As a member of the provincial legislative assembly I had something to do with bringing to the attention of the government the possibilities of this thousand acres of pasture land if it were irrigated. Not long ago a start was made; a few hundred acres of this land were placed under irrigation, and the results obtained have been simply amazing. This project is under the control of the provincial mental hospital, with the staff and patients doing the work from spring till fall. The mental hospital is responsible for the care ef the crops, but those crops have become so immense that even with all the stock on the farm and the population of three thousand people in the mental hospital, it is not possible to consume what is produced there. I should like to give one or two figures in connection with this project. I am not in a position this evening to give the exact number of acres under cultivation for the growing of vegetables and roots, but a very large part of the land being cultivated is used to grow oats, alfalfa and other fodder for the stock on the farm. There is a twenty-three acre field of oats which yielded a crop at the rate of 114 bushels to the acre. The alfalfa crop amounted to several tons per acre; I have not the exact figure per acre. Then we made a start in the growing of small fruits and vegetables, with these results:

This project has been under cultivation for only three or four years, but the results obtained already are almost beyond comprehension; it is necessary to go there in order to appreciate exactly what has been done. Since coming to eastern Canada I have heard critics in this house, more particularly those coming from Ontario, say that the western farmer is too lazy to go into mixed farming. It may not be known to many hon. members that in Saskatchewan there are large areas in which sufficient water cannot be obtained for domestic requirements and where stock cannot therefore be raised. In other regions the quality of the soil and the absence of moisture are such that coarse grain cannot grow and mature. However, in some sections we have made vast strides in regard to mixed farming. For the first time Alberta has led all the provinces in hog production. Saskatchewan has made progress also, and in a few moments I propose to read a few figures with respect to what has been done in that province. Before doing so, however, I would warn eastern farmers that if their advice were taken literally, the production of hogs, cattle, sheep, horses, eggs, butter and cheese in western Canada would swamp the market and break prevailing prices.
Now just a word with regard to stock production in Saskatchewan, as between 1941

Now just another figure or two with respect to another form of production. speechtext:
I am very glad to have that assurance from the minister. This branch of the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve was established at the port of Saint John two decades ago. In the years preceding the war many of our boys joined this unit. They obtained useful training there, and made friendships within the unit, with the result that an esprit de corps has been developed. The unit has its own traditions. It has become part of our community life. Many of the boys, both officers and men, enlisted when war was declared, and have given good accounts of themselves.
Since the outbreak of the war the work of the unit has been carried on in a more intensive manner. While I am glad to have the minister's assurance, I must tell him that if the report which has appeared in the press turns out to be true, and the unit is removed from Saint John, such action on the part of the government would be deeply, and I submit justly, resented by practically everybody in the community, irrespective of poli-

The Budget-Mr. Hazen
tical affiliations. I must confess I was pretty hot under the collar when I read the item in the newspaper. I hope it will not prove to be true.
The feelings of resentment and indignation engendered by the report are not based on any loss of business, or any loss of dollars and cents. They arise from feelings which lie closer to the human heart and which., in the long run, are of greater importance. They are engendered by the fact that our people live in an old but modern and active sea port, one which has generations of sea tradition behind it, that has known great days in the past when it was the fifth largest shipowning port in the world1, and it looks forward, too, to greater days in the future, as our country develops. Our people regard this unit as part of its community life and part of its sea tradition.
I should think the feelings of the people of Toronto would be very much hurt if they were informed that the Queen's Own, or some other militia unit belonging to that city, were to be moved bag and baggage to the city of Quebec. The people of Ottawa would be equally disturbed if they were to hear that the Governor General's Foot Guards were to be transferred to Truro. And1 I say that the people of Saint John are very perturbed over this report.
There appeared in the Telegraph-Journal of Saint John, New Brunswick, on Tuesday last, an editorial, which I believe voices the feelings of the people of that city to a considerable extent. It is headed "Prevent this Injury", and states:
The incomplete news received as regards what is to happen to H.M.C.S. Brunswicker gives rise to serious misgivings. If things actually proceed as they appear to be shaping, it will mean that the training of R.C.N.V.R. ratings will cease, or almost cease, here and be moved to a Nova Scotian port, leaving few more than a recruiting staff. The news is indefinite, but it contains a threat that hon. Angus L. Macdonald, Minister of Defence for Naval Services, has in mind some plan that, as at present represented, will be definitely detrimental to Saint John. No reason has been given.
This, coming on top of the establishment of a naval signals training school in an inland town in the province of Quebec, seems to challenge every New Brunswick member of parliament and senator to combine and make their influence felt to prevent the plan being carried through. New Brunswick has no desire to attack Mr. Macdonald, but it has not the slightest intention of sitting down and permitting neglect and discrimination. When these are foreshadowed they must be prevented. During war time we all have enough to do to fight the enemy, and in New Brunswick at least we have more sense than to wish to join battle with a minister of the crown. However, if the latter starts some-72537-801
thing harmful to us, he will find us not backward in self-defence. Therefore it is to be hoped that joint action by all New Brunswick representatives in Ottawa, irrespective of party, will succeed in averting that which has the makings of very hard feelings.
When the war appropriation bill was before the house in committee last May and the minister's estimates were being considered, we were informed by him that $635,500 was being set aside for the erection of piers, buildings and the provision of other services in Saint John. Of this amount, $190,000 was a carryover from the previous year. This amount was small compared with the $7,500,000 which we were told was to be spent in Halifax, with the $4,469,000 which we were told was to be spent at the Sydney base and with the $2,500,000 which we were told was to be spent at Esquimalt. We were not told on that occasion about the $20,000,000-I have not the exact figures-that was to be spent at Deep Brook in Annapolis county, Nova Scotia. No mention of the fact was made that a development was to take place there, and as far as I can recollect no mention was made of the fact that $2,624,000 was to be spent in constructing a naval establishment at the inland town of St. Hyacinthe in Quebec, although the plans for these establishments must have been well under way at that time. The Minister of National Defence for Naval Services told us at that time that an administration building was to be built at Saint John at a cost of $25,000.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, so far the debate on the budget has provided each of the political parties in the house with an opportunity to set forth its monetary policy. I wish to speak for a few moments on the amendment to the amendment, particularly the first paragraph. I gathered from listening to the debate that all members of the house are agreed on certain points. I think we are all agreed that money is the medium for the exchange of goods and services and that the chief function of money in our national economy is to provide for an equitable exchange of those goods and services. I think we are agreed also that the success of any policy can be determined by the degree to which it succeeds in distributing these goods and services equitably.
At least four of the parties in the house have expressed their opinion regarding the soundness of the government's policy. I think the financial critic of the opposition is more optimistic about the soundness of the present government policy than is the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley). For that matter the Minister of Finance and the financial critic expressed some concern over the fact that last year it was necessary to borrow so heavily from the banks-1983,000,000, according to the minister's statement, $790,000,000 of which was borrowed from the private chartered banks. The hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) made no distinction between the money bor-

rowed from the Bank of Canada and that borrowed from the private banks. To him they were all just bank borrowings. I think the minister made it clear that he would have preferred to borrow more than he did from the Bank of Canada. I am sure if I am wrong in that he will set me right. I think I am correct in saying that he made it clear to us that the only reason why he could not borrow more from the Bank of Canada was that for every $1,000,000 he borrowed from the Bank of Canada the private banks would thereby be automatically able to advance by way of credit another $10,000,000, thereby multiplying the danger of inflation tenfold. Apparently the policy he followed was that of borrowing $1,000,000 from the Bank of Canada, and then taking up by government loan the $10,000,000 which the private banks could advance by way of credit on that Bank of Canada security. The chief concern of both the minister and the financial critic of the opposition regarding this transaction was the inherent danger of inflation. Another danger brought to the attention of this house by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) was that while to-day the interest charges on those loans are comparatively low-I think the minister said 2-6 per cent over the whole borrowings-we have no assurance that in the post-war period we shall not be obliged to revert to pre-war interest rates. We have no assurance that the taxpayers of this country will not be required in future years to pay higher interest rates than those prevailing to-day.
The picture as I have been able to see it, listening to the minister and to his critic, is this: It is not this government which in the final analysis determines the monetary policy of the country. In so far as the minister is restrained from borrowing from the bank of Canada because of the power which that borrowing gives to the private banks, to that extent the private banks are determining the monetary policy of this government. I do not think any hon. member can escape that conclusion. There may be differences as to what the remedy is. We in the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation have attempted to make it quite clear and to set forth in our amendment that as far as we are concerned we do not believe that any control short of the socialization of the entire banking system which will make the branches of the private banks branches of the government-owned Bank of Canada will solve the difficulties of our monetary policy and make money what it should be, the servant and not the master of our economy.

The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy
There is a second feature of the government's fiscal policy with which we are in disagreement, namely, the level at which the government has found it necessary to freeze wages and farm prices. I know the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) does not like to hear that word "freeze."

speechtext:
Without going into details let us review a few of the most significant facts, and I ask the Minister of Labour to correct me in this wherein I am wrong.
The dominion bureau of statistics sets forth, as this house has already been told, the fact that in 1941, eighty-three per cent of the wage-earners of Canada were in receipt of incomes of less than $1,500 a year, or $29 a week. The next fact is that there are many industries, both essential and non-essential which were depressed and in which wages had not been adjusted at the time the government's policy came into effect. There is still a very wide variation in the amounts paid to workers by way of cost-of-living bonus oftentimes in industries in the same location and engaged on the same type of work. Increases or adjustments have been made from time to time by the war labour boards but I submit that in by far the majority of those instances the adjustments have been made where labour has been sufficiently organized to bring the case of the workers to the attention of the minister and his department, and in all those industries where labour is unorganized, where the workers have no spokesman to present their case to the minister or his department, wages still remain low. The argument which we hear raised particularly when large numbers of workers are involved is that adjustments will wreck the government's price-fixing and wage-fixing policy. I submit that any government policy which has to depend for its success upon the government's ability to keep vast numbers of our workers and vast numbers of our farmers in receipt of incomes below minimum standards is socially unsound. That, to my mind, is the weakness of the present government policy regarding farm prices and labour. Its success depends upon the extent to which the government can succeed in keeping those who are in receipt of low incomes at that low income level.
There is not an hon. member who does not agree that some restraints are necessary to curb the purchasing power of consumers or to keep it in line with the supply of consumer goods. We all realize that workers would suffer probably more than anyone else should inflation take place. But I ask the government, is it necessary, in order to prevent inflation, to keep eighty-three per cent of our wage-earners in receipt of income lower than that accepted by the government itself as a minimum standard of living? Surely not. If consumer purchasing power must be restricted- and I agree that it should-certainly those restrictions should fall upon all citizens impartially. Taxation and compulsory saving do just that; they make the burden fall fairly impartially if the taxes are properly distributed. But keeping wages in one industry lower than wages in another, or keeping wages in one province lower than wages in another, does not distribute the restrictions equitably; it has just the opposite effect; it imposes a special set of restrictions upon those in the lower income brackets.
The threat of inflation is used, I fear, as a bogey to prevent equitable adjustments of wages and prices. If we are not willing to make those necessary adjustments on purely humanitarian grounds, surely it has been made quite clear by private hon. members in this house that this policy, by reducing production, is defeating the very purpose we set out to achieve in our war effort. On this ground, if not on humanitarian grounds, I contend that we should find some way of preventing inflation without having recourse to a policy of depressing so many of our people.
I do not agree with or accept the remedy proposed by the financial critic of the opposition, the hon. member for Danforth.	He
advocates reducing the tax rates and spreading the tax. I should want to know what taxes are to be reduced and where they are to be spread before I could accept that solution.	He
quoted from the New York Herald Tribune, and I take it he thereby sanctioned the quotation he read and committed himself and his party to the opinion expressed therein. This is what he gave as the reason for absenteeism. It is reported in Hansard, at page 1078:
"It is that we are spoiling our war workers with wages which most of them never before dreamed of earning."
Later on he says that absenteeism-
. . . arises because the taxation brought down in the last budget has made it easy for labour to stay away from their places of employment. . . .
The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy

I submit that these charges against the industrial workers of this country in war time are serious charges when laid by the financial critic of the newly formed or re-organized Progressive Conservative party, whose proclaimed mission was to bring light and hope to the masses of our people. I shall make no comment except to say that I cannot accept that as an explanation of the cause, the fundamental cause of absenteeism and reduced production.
One other remark made by the hon. member for Danforth calls for consideration. He exhorted the wage-earner to build up for himself "a cushion" for the after-the-war period. Had the hon. member already abandoned hope of his party ever being returned to power? Surely he was not thinking in terms of that marvellous Winnipeg programme when he spoke of the necessity of cushions to help us over depression, unemployment and so forth. Was he conceding the next election to the Liberals when he made that statement?
In speaking on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, I tried to show that in Great Britain they had controlled inflation without having recourse to the freezing of wages and prices to the extent that it has been done in this country. The minister was not satisfied with some of my explanations. Let us get the record straight. I have looked into this matter as carefully as I possibly can. This is what I find.
From the beginning of the war to the end of 1941, wage rates increased in Great Britain between 26 and 27 per cent. In 1941 wage rate increases added eight million dollars a week to the national payroll. Wage rate increases plus the longer hours of work and the greater number of workers increased the total weekly earnings of the people by 42 per cent.

That is the point the minister was making, and I want to put this straight for my benefit as well as his. In 1942 wage rate increases added another $6,400,000 to the weekly earnings of approximately six million workers. Notwithstanding this vast increase in total wage-earner purchasing power the cost of living in Great Britain has risen only three per cent since the end of 1940. Since May, 1941, there has been virtually no increase in the cost of living. In the light of those facts I find it hard to believe that the government's wage and price fixing policy is designed exclusively for the prevention of inflation.
There are a few other matters in the budget on which I should like to comment. One is the change introduced in the income tax payable by officers in the armed forces. I confess I was unable to understand what the changes meant, and therefore I wrote to a friend of mine, an army officer who was a university graduate in mathematics. I concluded that no one who was not a specialist in mathematics could possibly interpret the regulations that the minister brought down. This is what my friend wrote in reply:
I think that the attitude of the officers in this centre towards Mr. Ilsley's proposals could be summed up in two words, "incredibly stupid". We cannot understand why Mr. Ilsley found it necessary to create a Chinese puzzle in order to provide some measure of relief for junior officers.
As far as I can discover, the net result of those changes is that a few first-class warrant officers will pay a small income tax. Junior officers will receive relief to the tune of $150 or possibly $200 per year.	Captains will
receive a slightly reduced income rate, and all above the rank of captain will not be affected by the changes.
There are one or two things the minister should have kept in mind in this connection. In all fairness to these men we must recognize that many of them have assumed their present responsibilities at some sacrifice. In many cases that I know of personally there was considerable sacrifice. I think we can accept the statement that the salary an officer receives does not necessarily indicate a purchasing power of that sum. A salary of $3,000 in that position is equivalent, I am informed, to about $2,400 in civil life. Officers in the armed forces are the victims of a racket as far as clothes are concerned. I think every army officer in this country will agree that the prices being charged to officers for uniforms are unwarrantably high. They are the victims of another playful habit that Ottawa has, that of changing the regulations frequently as to what an officer shall or shall not wear. These regulations are changed so frequently that considerable expense is involved on the part of the officer in trying to keep up with the changing regulations.
The suggestion I would make in regard to this particular class is that the military pay and allowances of all ranks up to and including a first lieutenant be totally exempt from income tax, and that the tax on officers' pay above that rank be on a graded scale in accordance with the spread between their pay and that received by a first lieutenant.

I am informed not only by officers but by privates that that is the situation. I find that my own constituents cannot talk to me about what is happening, cannot express any criticism of government policy on account of obligations they have been required to assume.
I am not sure that the distinction between those serving at home and those serving abroad is fully justified, certainly not in the light of experience up to the present time. Most of those men serving at home are at the government's disposal; the reason why they are not overseas is that the government wants them here. A great many of those who have gone overseas have been occupying administrative positions in England not radically different from those occupied by the men who have remained on this side.
A third matter on which I wish to offer some comment is the change in the regulations regarding the encouragement given to producers of oil. I brought this matter up in the house on several occasions last year. The point I am interested in is that we are not producing a very great quantity of oil in this country, and that we have resources which we are not developing. If these changes will facilitate the development of our own resources, I am sure we will pardon the minister, in order that we may get that vital necessity at the present time, even if some of these exemptions go to vested interests. In Alberta is produced ninety per cent of Canada's total production of oil, coming largely from the Turner oil fields. The Calgary Oil Bulletin, a fairly authentic publication, gives this information:
A week ago there were seventeen actively drilling wells in that field, whereas a year ago
there were thirty-four. We were producing in February 25,000 barrels of crude oil per day as against 28,000 a year ago, a decrease of
3.000	barrels per day.
Notwithstanding the fact that there are 100 proven drill sites withheld and undrilled in that field by one major oil interest alone, we are to-day importing into western Canada from
200.000	to 300,000 barrels of crude oil a month. Seventy per cent of the oil of Alberta is produced from the independent wells, operated by independent companies which are financed through the sale of royalties, for the most part in the industrial centres of Canada. When the oil controller's regulations were put into effect last year the men who had been devoting their time to the sale of these royalties and the promotion of the development of the independent wells of that district were refused anything higher than category A, the same category that was given pleasure drivers. I personally went to the oil controller in connection with the matter, but his statement was that we did not need that oil; that it was not a question of a shortage of oil but entirely a question of transportation. Apparently to-day the ministry has taken a different stand and is bringing in concessions that will encourage the development of oil in our own country. I want to ask the minister concerned how he can justify the granting of only category A, the category of pleasure drivers, to men who are engaged solely in the promotion of the production of oil in Canada. Is there any other reason behind that action? Is it that these oil interests object to the independent companies developing the oil wells of Alberta? That, I submit, is a question which requires some investigation.
I had hoped to make some comment on the situation with regard to cobalt. A month ago I asked, through the medium of the order paper for official information. My motion was adopted on February 22, but so far the only information I have is what I myself have been able to gather. Therefore I should like to be corrected if in any particular my statements are wrong. My information is that to-day there is an abundance of cobalt in northern Ontario; that we are importing cobalt for refining in this country; that the owners of these properties in northern Ontario can secure neither permission nor priority rights to develop these properties; and that one mining corporation is gradually buying up all these properties. I asked for information with regard to a report made by a Mr. Reid, of the Ontario department of mines, which I understand was submitted to the metals controller last October. For some reason that report was withdrawn and was not published, and I am told that the revised edition of the report was
The Budget-Mr. Kinley

made public only recently. I asked, through the order paper, what essential difference there was between the original and the revised report, and I was told there was none. I should like to ask the minister if it is not true that to-day there is only one small refinery for cobalt in northern Ontario; that the producers of that metal must accept a relatively small share of the returns, and that there was a recommendation in the first report that the government should assist in the erection of a refinery for cobalt. I understand there is no such recommendation in the revised report.

maintopic: TAXING OF POOLS-STATEMENT OF MR. SPEAKER AS TO QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the thought uppermost in the minds of all of us each and every day is with regard to the progress of the war, more particularly with regard to our duty in this parliament. We are all concerned about the fortunes of our arms in the field, with their support and maintenance; and at the same time we must invoke the aid of science, industry and labour to the fullest possible extent in order that our country may become powerful and strong. Then we must use this power in the most intensive way in order to help our allies, the united nations, to achieve victory and thus secure the safety of the land.
It seems to me that the budget presented a little over a week ago will give to many the best possible picture of how great is the war effort of this country. It gives us a record of the achievements of the year just coming to a close, showing what our people paid in taxes and what they provided the government by way of loans. With balances it gives us the information so that we. can go ahead intelligently to the year ahead. The budget also provides estimates and commitments, and shows us that during the year to come our burden will be greater than, at any time in our history.
This budget has been before the house for over a week, and in that time has been criticized by the opposition and commended by hon. members on the government benches. The hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris), in a long, exhaustive analysis, made some criticisms, and perhaps made some suggestions of value, which will have salutary effect upon the administration. He was most cordial about it all-and it seems to me he might well be, a man who had two weddings in his family in one day, just before his speech in the house. A man in that position might very well be cordial.
It is the duty of the opposition to be critical, and it is expected that the weak

points or those points which can be improved will be dwelt upon by opposition members. It is in that way we bring out the truth, and make stronger our efforts in the interests of the whole dominion. It seems to me, however, that nothing seriously wrong was found with the budget. The fault-finding was of a general nature. The opposition offered no amendment. I believe that members of the Progressive Conservative party accepted the budget, not as one of desire but as one of necessity, and that they were proud of the accumulated results of the effort of our country. Therefore that party did not oppose the budget.
There are three common faults oppositions find with budgets. First, there is excessive taxation; second, hard times-and that is something which is always held against a government. I think we can say that from a commercial point of view there are no hard times at present in Canada. Third, extravagance is a fault which can be well found in, respect of any budget or any government. Strange to say, however, from the groups in the far corner of the house came two amendments, both of which were unique in that they asked for more expenditure and more taxation on the people of Canada.
I admit that the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), in the earnest and forceful way wherewith he presents his ideas on money, offered an amendment which he believes is an easy way to finance the war. I am afraid that way is too easy to be of any abiding benefit. To accept it in any degree would be a sign of weakness, not of strength-and we want Canada to be a strong country.
Then, a subamendment was moved by the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, and this subamendment is something along the same lines, except that the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation wants to nationalize the banks. They believe we should have government banks doing the business of the country. Well, from a general point of view it would appear to me that, whatever virtue there might be in change, now is the time not to try any change; rather we should have stability and unity to carry on the war.
I have no brief for the banks, but I think that along with the merchants and the people in charge of industry in Canada, in the past decade the banks have done a fairly good job. I can recall the days of the depression when the banks of the United States had to close their doors. They had financial chaos, but in Canada the banks carried on and were a

The Budget-Mr. Kinley
source of strength. But we must realize also that our banks succeed outside Canada, and it is a good thing when that condition prevails. The banks of Canada have agencies in the West Indies, Europe, Great Britain and even in New York, the centre of the money market of the world. I always thought that Canada was rather proud of her banking system, and that it was doing a good service and serving Canada in a healthy way.
We have the Bank of Canada, which is our national bank. It is a government institution. The Bank of Canada does control the activities of the other banks. If we had a government bank in every town in Canada we would have a political institution, and would thereby increase bureaucracy. While now a merchant or citizen can go to one bank and, if he is not satisfied, can go to another, if we had a government bank there would be no other to go to, and as a result he would have perhaps to submit to the arrogance and indolence of public officials.
It may be that the banks have a monopoly. I know one thing: They do not quarrel in public, and that is a pretty good sign. But if our friends in the far corner want banks, why do they not start banks in this country?
