speechtext:
What about the Alberta
bank charter?

maintopic: TAXING OF POOLS-STATEMENT OF MR. SPEAKER AS TO QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext:
A bill came in from Alberta during tire last parliament to create a provincial bank. It came before the banking and commerce committee. What did they want? They did not want to conform to the Bank Act of this country. They did not want to conform to controls of the government. They wanted a special act with special privileges in order that they could carry on banking as they would like it. There is no reason why provinces in Canada cannot start banks, and there is no reason why they could not carry them on successfully. The hon. member (Mr. Noseworthy) who preceded me spoke about borrowing money from the private banks. It is better to borrow money from the people, but the government used the private banks in an emergency, and borrowed at a price below the cost of doing business. Even if we had government banks I believe that the cost of doing business would be higher than it is at present, with the chartered banks, and that it would be just one step toward that state of socialism for which our hon. friends hope. At any rate the Bank Act is due for review, I believe, next year.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) does not like the profit motive in industry. May I point out that in a few weeks time seeding operations will be in order. The farmers of western Canada will have to plant. I wonder if they are going to plant their farms for fun?

maintopic: TAXING OF POOLS-STATEMENT OF MR. SPEAKER AS TO QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: That is what they have been doing for the past five or six years.

maintopic: TAXING OF POOLS-STATEMENT OF MR. SPEAKER AS TO QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext:
Or I wonder if they will expect a profit. There is a bit of a gamble in connection with it. If they get rain; if they have the proper conditions of atmosphere; if they have good soil, they can expect a good crop and an increase. If they do not get it, we shall hear about it in this parliament. Furthermore, I want to say the western corporations are very astute. For years they have been able to manoeuvre themselves into a position where they did not need to assume their obligations by way of payment of income taxes.
This afternoon the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar asked whether the wheat pools in western Canada would pay income taxes to the federal government. He probably knew that the Department of Justice had given a decision that the pools were not real cooperatives. I believe the matter is likely to be referred to the courts. The other day the hon. member for Danforth sang a swansong in connection with the taxes to be paid by the so-called cooperatives. I suppose that is a connection that they made at the Winnipeg convention. It seems to me that when they ask the government whether these organizations are to have to pay an income tax, we can assume that they have profits. If they have no profits, why worry about it?
We all realize that real cooperatives will not be asked to pay an income tax by the government of Canada. The hon. member apparently forgets that in 1929 there was an amendment to the income tax act in connection with the cooperatives in western Canada and that the word "reserves" was inserted. The result has been the piling up of millions of dollars of reserves in western Canada by the wheat pools and they have no income tax. I think it is only fair and reasonable that these people should assume their fair share of responsibility. The other day the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) had something to say about cooperatives. He quoted from a letter, although he did not say from whom it had been received. I should like to repeat part of this quotation as reported at page 1168 of Hansard:
Last year these creameries paid five cents a pound less for butter fat than the farmers were
The Budget-Mr. Kinley

getting in northwestern Nova Scotia where the great Scotsburn cooperative creamery is the yardstick for the price.
I have nothing against the Scotsburn creamery because it is a well run organization in Pictou county, but I think my hon. friend is wrong. My information is that the Tatama-gouche creamery is privately owned and is one of the largest in Nova Scotia, doing about three times the business done by the Scotsburn creamery. It must compete with the Scotsburn creamery, otherwise they would not hold their business. The Tatamagouche jreamery is about twenty-five miles from the Scotsburn creamery. To say that private business is not able to compete is not true. The same thing prevails all over Nova Scotia in connection with creameries. There is a cooperative at Antigonish, and as a rule their prices are lower than those paid in western Nova Scotia. The government is running three creameries in Cape Breton, and their prices are usually lower than the prices paid in Middleton and western Nova Scotia. This I have in a telegram from an informed source in Nova Scotia.
I believe in cooperative creameries for the farmer because I think they are fine things, but we must realize that the private creamery has an extra burden to carry in the payment of income tax. When a member from Nova Scotia comes to this house and tries to teil us that private industry in Nova Scotia is being backed to the wall, that it cannot exist and pay the prices as against the cooperative creameries, he is not telling a story that is borne out by the facts.
We hear a great deal about profits. I do not contend that profits are divine, but I think they have a place in the divine order of things. There is not a flower or a tree that does not profit in increase by reason of the elements and by reason of its life. In fact, all life must have an increase and profit or it will die. I have no apologies to make for seeming to try to reach out to the spiritual because that is one of the four freedoms.
I am free to say that I am not against big business as such, but I am against monopolies. No country ever became great without big business. While the capitalist system is not perfect, it has served the world for many years and has made Great Britain, the United States and Canada great free countries that we hope will prevail in the struggle in which they are now engaged. I do not think it is the capitalist system that hurts the world; I think it is greed. Greed is a human characteristic; it has not to do with the capitalist system alone.
I think greed will be found in every system, 
and to control greed and those who would control others seems to me to be our object in the future.
It is not the capitalist system that hurts; it is the abuse of that system. War has purged the capitalist system and it has its benefits in that regard. No man can get rich during this war, no matter what services he renders. We hope that the cleansing that goes on, the cleansing that must come to every system from time to time, will prove of salutary benefit.
Our hon. friends talk about New Zealand. Distant fields look greener, and my hon. friends go about as far away from Canada as they can for their example. New Zealand is a little country of 103,723 square miles, half as large as Manitoba. It has a population of
1,500,000	and is completely surrounded by water. It has one government. It is a country largely engaged in pastoral pursuits, and the same viewpoint is largely prevalent. It is not hard for these people to divide their money and services among themselves as they want to, but it must be realized that they make their money by shipping their goods to capitalist England and other countries in the world.
The minister in his budget asked the people to work and save. That is an old and simple rule, but considerable resolution and discipline are required to carry it out. I read a story once of an ancient sultan who, when he sent his couriers over his empire, would seal his letters with a signet ring on which was this inscription-I translate into English-"You cannot go astray on a straight road." As far as work and save is concerned, the road is straight, but it is a hard road and I want to sound this note of warning. While the people will work and save, they also expect the government to work and save. They expect everybody down to the smallest official in the most remote place to save as much as they can and to stop improvident expenditure wherever possible. I do not mean that there should be cheese-paring, because the people of this country expect a little dignity and colour in their war programme and in the conduct of their officials. It will be recalled that Donald Gordon, chairman of the wartime prices and trade board, called on the housewives of this country to check on the merchants and storekeepers in order that the price ceiling would be maintained. I wrote a letter to the press in my riding telling my people that they should keep their eyes open and that if they saw extravagance or improvidence they should let me know and I would very soon bring it to the attention of the government.

The Budget-Mr. Kinley
While we are interested in the war effort, there is also a great wave of public opinion in this and other countries that we should be preparing for the future. It seems to me that there is to-day an atmosphere of good-will among the united nations which should be taken advantage of so that when the war is over and conditions are confused we shall be able to have something planned and ready. I think this atmosphere began with the Atlantic charter. That was followed by the mutual aid agreement between the United States and Great Britain. I wish to quote one article of that agreement which is contained in a publication put out by the magazine Fortune. It is a fine piece of institutional advertising for future unity. Article VII of the mutual aid agreement, February 23, 1942, reads:
In the final determination of the benefits to be provided to the United States of America by the government of the United Kingdom in return for aid furnished under the act of congress of March 11, 1941, the terms and conditions thereof shall be such as not to burden commerce between the two countries but to promote mutually advantageous economic relations between them and the betterment of world-wide economic relations. To that end, they shall include provision for agreed action by the United States of America and the United Kingdom, open to participation by all other countries of like mind, directed to the expansion, by appropriate international and domestic measures, of production, employment, and the exchange and consumption of goods, which are the material foundations of the liberty and welfare of all peoples; to the elimination of all forms of discriminatory treatment in international commerce, and to the reduction of tariffs and other trade barriers; and, in general, to the attainment of all the economic objectives set forth in the joint declaration made on August 12, 1941, by the President of the United States of America and the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom.
That is a very fine paragraph, but I submit that the text of it is to be found in these words:
.	.	. but to promote mutually advantageous
economic relations between them. . . .
Note the words, "mutually advantageous". A pretty safe statement. It brings to our minds that notwithstanding the good feeling that exists to-day, in the future practically everything will have to be justified upon economic grounds, and not only shall we have to show that a thing is mutually advantageous internationally, but here in Canada, for instance, we shall have to show that a project is mutually advantageous to the different groups and sections of this country before we shall be able to make trade treaties with other countries. I believe that it will take all the ingenuity and all the good-will we have to prevent economic nationalism from arising in
the days to come, and it is just as well to start early and to have the people informed. While leaders and governments make agreements, they have the habit of passing. We had an example of that after the last war when the idealism of President Wilson failed to come to fruition partly on account of what happened at Versailles and also on account of what happened in his own country. The only safe thing to do is to have the people well informed because, unlike leaders and governments, the people are always there and their will must prevail. Therefore let us start now and see to it that everybody in this country is informed about the good-will and cooperation that we all expect in the world that is to be.
I think the members of the house should tell here the story of what is best for their own districts. Since I come from the maritime provinces my thoughts naturally turn to the sea. I believe that as it was in the past so it will be in the future, and that if Nova Scotia and the maritimes are to prosper as a part of Canada it will be by reason of their activities on the sea. The Sirois report gives us a colourful account of the economy of Nova Scotia in what they call the golden age, in the days of the sailing ship. Nova Scotia was then outstanding as a result of her sea-borne transportation. It was then that we had banks, too. It was then that we had a balanced economy and were the most successful part of Canada. There is no reason why that cannot happen again. But after the passing of the wooden ship Nova Scotia never had a chance with sea-going vessels. The coasting trade is the nursery of the seagoing trade, and Nova Scotia never had a real chance even at her coasting trade. In 1894 the British Merchant Shipping Act was passed, section 736 of which reads:
The legislature of a British possession, may, by any act or ordinance, regulate the coasting trade of that British possession subject in every case to the following conditions:-
(a)	The act or ordinance shall contain a suspending clause providing that the act or ordinance shall not come into operation until her majesty's pleasure thereon has been publicly signified in the British possession in which it has been passed:
(b)	The act or ordinance shall treat all British ships (including the ships of any other British possession) in exactly the same manner as ships of the British possession in which it is made:
(c)	Where by treaty made before the passing of the Merchant Shipping (Colonial) Act, 1869 (that is to say, before the thirteenth, day of May eighteen hundred and sixty-nine), her majesty has agreed to grant to any ships of any foreign state any rights or privileges in respect of the coasting trade of any British possession, those rights and privileges shall be enjoyed by
The Budget-Mr. Kinley

those ships for so long as her majesty has already agreed or may hereafter agree to grant the same, anything in the act or ordinance to the contrary notwithstanding.
That was the Merchant Shipping Act of 1894. Ministers went from Canada to Great Britain on various occasions in order to get control of the coasting trade. In 1931 came the Statute of Westminster, one clause of which reads:
Without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing provisions of this act, sections 735 and 736-
Section 736 is the one I quoted.

of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1894, shall be construed as though reference therein to the legislature of a British possession did not include reference to the parliament of a dominion.
That meant that the coasting trade of Canada would be in the hands of the Canadian government. That measure was passed on December 11, 1931. On December 10, just before the passing of the Statute of Westminster, the British commonwealth merchant shipping agreement was approved. It took away all that was given to Canada by the Statute of Westminster in so far as coasting shipping was concerned.
Part IY-Equal Treatment . . .
Article 11.-While each part of the British commonwealth may regulate its own coasting trade, it is agreed that any laws or regulations from time to time in force for that purpose shall treat all ships registered in the British commonwealth in exactly the same manner as ships registered in that part, and not less favourably in any respect than ships of any foreign country.
Article 12.-Nothing in the present agreement shall be deemed

(i)	to derogate from the right of every part of the commonwealth to impose customs tariff duties on ships built outside that part; or
(ii)	to restrict the right of the government of each part of the commonwealth to give financial assistance to ships registered in that part or its right to regulate the sea fisheries of that part.
The last paragraph is a little difficult to understand. Article 27 states:
This agreement shall apply to all territories administered under the authority of the government of any part of the commonwealth and to ships registered there, or in any foreign port of registry, and fulfilling the requirements as to ownership set out in article 2 (1).
It can be seen that there is no nursery here for the coasting trade, which would have been the start of a revival of shipping. With the advance of steam and the building of iron ships, Nova Scotia shipping gradually disappeared. The United States has always protected her coastal trade by means of her coastal regulations. She has a higher standard of 
living than any other country in the world. One of the things this government should do when negotiating the next reciprocity agreement with the United States is to ask for reciprocity in the coasting trade. The St. Lawrence waterway will be built one of these days; Fort William at the head of the lakes will be an ocean port, and all Canadians will be interested in our coasting trade. It seems to me that for the promotion of good-will between ourselves and' the United States, reciprocity in the coasting trade as between the two countries would be highly desirable. Now is the time for Canada to become sea-minded. Men from the Pacific coast, from Saskatoon, Winnipeg, Toronto and every port of Canada are on our coast at the present time manning the ships of the Canadian navy. The crews of our navy now number 52,000 men; there are 38,000 of our seamen in the merchant marine, and 22,000 who have foreign-going identification cards. To-day Canada is building ships. We are told that ninety-seven have been built in Canadian shipyards during the war, but only seven of them are operated through the Parke Steamship government owned company. For the dominion the others are operated and, I think, owned by the United States and other powers. I believe that shortage of crews has something to do with the limited number of ships we are operating, also that it is the intention that Canada shall operate twenty or thirty more next year. It is also my belief that we must take care to see to it that when this war is over we are operating enough ships to absorb the men who are now in the navy and in the merchant marine; that the future young citizens of Nova Scotia will be able to make a living on the sea, and that Canada will have a merchant marine of which she may be proud.
At this point I wish to say a word on behalf of the merchant marine. Herein is one fault I have to find with the budget. The losses of our merchant marine are upwards of a thousand men. Although I do not believe very much in tax exemptions, it seems to me, as a matter of right and equity, they should be extended to the men of the merchant marine as well as to the men in the armed forces. We call them our merchant navy. We have enough faith in the government to know that right will prevail, but right needs pressure and influence behind it if it is to prevail quickly.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that if you lived on the eastern coast of Canada and knew at first hand the privations and hazards which the men of the merchant navy are facing, you would say that they, too, deserve all we can give

The Budget-Mr. Roy
them, and that whatever exemptions go to the soldiers and the navy should go to the merchant marine.

Perhaps I may be allowed to finish. With the permission of the house I will continue. The deep-sea fishermen of Nova Scotia go out on the banks of the Atlantic and are subject every day to the hazards of the submarine. Not only do they not get exemption on income tax but they must pay on the part of their wages represented by the food which they eat aboard the ships on which they go. I believe an exemption in this particular was allowed to the merchant marine, and I think it should be granted also to the deep-sea fishermen, many of whom come from my riding.
I hope that in the future we shall have free trade in fish with the United States. We had it during the last war. There is a quota at the present time on Canadian fish, but I hope the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) will see to it that we get free entry of fish during the war, because then we shall be on the threshold of keeping it after the war is over and so extending the good-will which is so desirable.
The thought I wish to leave with the house is that Canada must become marine-minded. Our citizens must realize that this country faces two oceans, and that in the trade of the world transportation is one of the big factors. Although Great Britain always had an adverse balance of trade, she compensated for it with unseen sources of revenue, much of which was provided by her merchant marine, also by her great insurance companies and her investments all over the world. Do not forget that, after this war is over, the people of the maritimes will need to be reestablished. They are now in the navy, many of them as volunteers, and if the government does this in a way that will stimulate our marine, give us a good big merchant marine, and keep our navy going as part of the protection of Canada to maintain her dignity and prestige, it will be doing something in the interest of the maritime people of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I would have desired to offer some comments on this budget submitted to us by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley). But since the question of the St. Lawrence has arisen again in the press, in the Quebec legislature and also in this house I shall
postpone my remarks on the budget and shall rather make an attempt to make a survey of this situation.
Since last summer I have been under the impression that an inquiry was to be made by the government as to the activities of the corvette which was supposed to have escorted a boat called the Jean Briand from Rimouski to the north shore. But as far as I know we have had no report on the said inquiry, if there has been one. I should like to tell the house what information I have about this corvette so that people will be better at ease about it. It might also kill the rumours that are circulating.
At the time that three ships were sunk opposite Cap Chat in the first days of July the boat I just mentioned was carrying some sportsmen going on a fishing trip on the north shore. Said boat was escorted by a corvette as far as to the north shore, but if my information is correct, this corvette did not complete the fishing trip with the boat, but came back to the south shore. My information is that the boat was escorted at the request of the Postmaster General (Mr. Mulock) because it was carrying the mail to the north shore. However, the boat never dropped off the mail on her way on but proceeded to the fishing trip for quite a few days. That is the information I have, and I do not think it can be denied. The captain of that corvette was later transferred to a "Q" boat which had since disappeared with him. The late captain was not to be blamed for having gone with the boat I mentioned.
Now I should deal with the number of boats which have been sunk in the St. Lawrence. This is quite a delicate matter. Since last November the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) has made quite a few statements saying that only twenty ships have been sunk in the St. Lawrence. On March 10 at page 1129 of Hansard he is reported as saying:
I could make a statement to the house to-day merely repeating what I have already said several times, that our records show twenty merchant ships sunk in the gulf and river St. Lawrence in the year 1942.
On the next page the minister continues, saying:
I have stated several times that twenty merchant ships have been sunk in the St. Lawrence gulf and river during the navigation season of 1942 as a result of enemy action.
From those two quotations one observes that the minister mentioned "merchant" ships. And we know that there have been some war vessels, such as corvettes, destroyers
126S
The Budget-Mr. Roy

and different types of war vessels; I do not know how to call them exactly, but there seems to be a play on words. I do not say there is; I say there seems to be. There might be a way for the minister to explain his statement when he says the number is twenty, and Mr. Onesime Gagnon of the Quebec legislature may be right also when he declares that there were more than thirty ships sunk in the St. Lawrence river and gulf. I will explain that. The population along Gaspe and the north shore-the population I know, to which I belong-our sailors in that section are accustomed to consider the waters of that section w7here Newfoundland is located as the waters of the St. Lawrence, because Newfoundland is located right in the mouth of the gulf of St. Lawrence. That makes quite a wider area than if you take only the middle of the strait of Belle isle and the strait of Cabot. One can find there an explanation of the differences between the minister, the Hon. Mr. Gagnon and myself because I sincerely believe that more than twenty ships have been sunk in that section. I will give an explanation of that. I have here a list of quite a few ships which are supposed to have been sunk in different places around Newfoundland.

As I have said, it may be a matter of the interpretation of the delimitation of the waters, or it may be a matter of determining which of the various services was concerned. If ever we have a general inquiry to consider this whole question, I can tell the minister one figure that will come out of the bag; it will be thirty-seven ships, As I have said, all these may not be within the zone which is officially regarded by the government as the waters of the gulf of St. Lawrence.
I do not claim that my information is always complete, though unfortunately on many occasions in the past the information I had was quite true, as it was proved to be by events which occurred, which became known later. In any event a member has the right to consider and depend upon the best information he can get from reliable sources. On the other hand we sometimes get information which is not correct. Thus last year, after some sinkings in the St. Lawrence, I wrote a private letter to the three ministers of defence pointing out the weaknesses of the defence of the St. LawTrence. I told them that we should have some radio facilities, a telephone line on the coast, and that the most important means of fighting properly the submarines would be to get some bombers at Mont Joli and at Gaspe. I received a reply from which I should like to quote a part. Some information contained in the letter is supposed to be secret, though it is not much of a type of secrecy. Let me read this part of the letter, in order to indicate that the information we receive is not always accurate. Speaking about the St. Lawrence gulf and river, the letter says:
The area is regarded as one of extreme danger to enemy submarines venturing therein and one which can be given maximum protection at minimum effort, due to the closeness of shore bases.

The Budget-Mr. Roy
In view of what has happened in the St. Lawrence since that time I venture to suggest that this information was not quite accurate. This brings me to speak again about the weaknesses of our defence on the St. Lawrence. After those first sinkings in May and July, and after what happened in this house, I kept trying to bring to the attention of the people of Canada the negligence and indeed the selfishness of the government in regard to the situation in the St. Lawrence. After the house was adjourned early in August I went back to my constituency and kept silent, but I did witness what was going on. For example, in the latter part of July, shortly before I reached home, on a sunny day exactly at noon, at Griffon cove which is right opposite my home, a battle was engaged between a submarine and two corvettes. As the battle was starting Mr. Laurent Giroux, a building contractor, rushed to a telephone and called the Gaspe operator, telling her to pass the word to Gaspe military base, where we were supposed to have some bombers. As a matter of fact we have some there, because day and night we hear them roaring in the air. As I have said, that occurred exactly at noon. The battle went on between the submarine and the two corvettes; I am told that later on there were two submarines, but I am not sure of that. The battle went on until half-past one, or for one hour and a half. No help ever came from Gaspe, though the distance to Griffon cove as a bird would fly is only about six and a half miles. No plane went over the area where the battle took place until five o'clock the following morning. Apparently the few boats we had there were not given adequate support by our air force. There was another attack made on the morning of September 16, at ten minutes after six, at Mechins; another at seven-thirty in the morn. mg of September 11, at Cap Chat; another at two o'clock in the afternoon of a nice sunny day at Cap des Rosiers. The people down there know that our planes have never participated in any battle in the course of which ships have been sunk by enemy submarines; and our people wonder why those planes should be overheard day and night when nothing is going on, and that there are none to drop bombs on these submarines when there are fights going on and ships are sunk. That is hard for the people to understand. That is one reason why the people there are alarmed, and they wonder why the government does not take some steps to give better protection to the ships which are carrying supplies to our allies.
Let me give another example of the weakness of our defences in that area. On September 15 one submarine was seen only one mile from the lighthouse at Cap des Rosiers, at exactly eleven o'clock in the morning. The keeper of the lighthouse, Mr. Joseph Ferguson, telephoned right away to Captain Cote, who is in charge of what we call the A.D.C. and also in charge of the telephone exchange at Cap des Rosiers. He is also manager of the telephone exchange at that point. The same Mr. Ferguson telephoned to Fox River, to another man of the A.D.C., Mr. Walter Lequesne. He said he had seen & submarine exactly one mile northeast of the lighthouse, and had placed a board to indicate the right spot where he had noticed the submarine. That was exactly eleven o'clock in the morning. A few minutes later from the lighthouse a convoy could be seen coming up from the southeast, toward that very spot. It was evident that something was going to happen to the convoy when it would reach there. There is about ten miles as the bird would fly from Fox River to the place where the submarine had been seen and where two boats were sunk a few minutes later.
The young ladies of Mr. Walter Lequesne, through the call from Mr. Walter Ferguson of Cap des Rosiers, had been informed of the fact that the convoy was coming up, and that the submarine was there. These young ladies, and the young ladies of Mr. Albert Morris of Fox River, climbed up inside the church steeple to watch what was going to happen down there. A few minutes later the convoy was coming up, right on top of the submarine. The torpedoes started to run on the waves, and two ships went down. The first one was struck at 12.21 p.m. and the second one at 12.22 p.m. The first one went down at 12.28 p.m. and the second at 12.32 p.m. No aeroplane showed around there to help the corvettes. There were some corvettes and destroyers in the convoy. But why is it that the naval officers of the Gaspe base and all the men who could have taken care of the situation, and who are supposed to have the necessary powers to act by themselves, without being obliged to call for orders from Halifax or Quebec, did not give the proper orders to change the course of that convoy? They had plenty of time to do it. The civilian population knew what was about to happen. They were watching the events. It was only the navy and the air force which did not seem to be aware of those facts. There surely was a lack of organization. I could mention a few other events of that kind.
The Budget-Mr. Roy

As I said, this happened on September 15. Some two weeks later, after I was sure of all the facts, I came up to Ottawa. I wrote a letter to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) asking him to convene parliament in order to discuss the gravity of the situation in the St. Lawrence. To be fair to the Prime Minister I must say that quite a few days later he wrote me a kind letter giving me the assurance that something was to be done, that the question was getting all the attention of the government, and that all means would be taken to improve the situation in that area.
May I be allowed to show that some declarations are not always wise, before proceeding with what occurred at the time the Prime Minister wrote me this letter. I wish to recall the declaration of the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) on July 13, 1942. I find the minister's statement at page 4126 of Hansard, when he answers the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), and when he deals with a statement I had made the week before. This is what the minister said:
I am not ready to change the disposition of one ship of the Canadian Navy for him or all the questions he may ask from now until doomsday.
I was not asking anything for my own sake. It was not for my own sake that I was giving information about the situation there. I was asking for more and better means of defence, for more protection. It was not for myself.
At the time I received a letter from the Prime Minister I had the pleasure of learning -I cannot give the date, because I do not think it would be wise to do so-that an important step had been taken by the British Admiralty to give chase to these submarines in the St. Lawrence gulf. It was worth while to take these steps in order to meet the requirements of the situation, but at that time the battle of the St. Lawrence gulf was lost, through selfishness and lack of organization.
These very points I have mentioned, enlarged by a great number of rumours of all sorts, sometimes assumed fantastic proportions, and alarmed the people seriously. It is not only a question of the number of sinkings, but the point is that we could have saved some of those ships if we had adopted better means, and had paid more attention to them. That is the question. There is also the point of saving money for the country. Had we saved only five or ten ships out of those which had been sunk, and had those ships made only one more trip before the closing of navigation, we probably would not see so much war material on the sidings here and there. If

some hon. members travelled between Montreal and Quebec I am sure they must have seen tanks and other war materials lying there to rot, through lack of means to send them to the places where they are so badly needed.
Further, the people think that if the St. Lawrence protection had been better organized last year, and if better protection had been given to our ships for the maintenance of that water route, there would not have been so much harm done to the harbours of Montreal and Quebec. They claim that the single-track railroad going to Halifax has been overloaded because of all the materials which have to be transported. They claim this water route deserves to be better protected, that it is the cheapest route, the shortest one, and the one with the greatest capacity for transporting materials overseas.
I now quote from an editorial appearing on Monday, March 10, in the Quebec Chronicle Telegraph. This is the last part of it:
The St. Lawrence is a strategic factor of first-rate importance in the battle of supplies, as we have said before. It ought to be kept open and in use and there is no reason why it cannot be kept open and in use with reasonable safety-as much safety as can be claimed for any other Atlantic route. Hon. Angus Macdonald apparently prefers the easier way and the Ottawa Journal and St. Thomas Times-Journal are quite willing to let him take it without question. We are sorry but, even at the risk of irritating the former or of being disciplined at the behest of the latter, we cannot let so vital an issue go by default.
That is the opinion of business men and of the population in Quebec. That is why you hear so much talk there.

Is this another threat from the minister to try to prevent the disclosing of facts that have been hidden from the population of this country? I am going to say this as long as I feel sure that it will not give information to the enemy. I believe I am doing my duty. Conditions would be better if the minister of the navy had paid more attention to what was told him. It would also have been better not to write letters such as the one I have mentioned which I received from one minister last summer to the effect that this section was the most dangerous for the enemy venturing therein and that it could be given the maximum protection with the

The Budget-Mr. Lizotte
minimum effort. That is the sort of declaration that was made to me last summer when I was trying to do my duty as a good citizen. I was told by the minister last year that he was not going to move one of his boats for my sake or because of my asking. It is things like that which have aroused the population of Quebec and myself and made us lose confidence in the minister. We know that these things are going on as we have witnessed them every day. We know what it means to the cause we are supporting at the cost of so many sacrifices.
I think it is important that if we should know the exact number of ships which have been sunk in the St. Lawrence, there are yet more other important matters which should be investigated in order to bring about better conditions next summer. Therefore, I submit respectfully that there should be a complete inquiry made by a royal commission so that the population, may be exactly informed, and all responsibilities established.

Mr. Chairman, lest the house be apprehensive I would state that I have no intention of speaking about U-boats which have visited the St. Lawrence during last year. It is a most important question and a fitting subject for a special debate after the adoption of the budget. I would fain, at this late hour, risk spoiling the sleep and repose of the hon. members of this house who well deserve their rest.
Ever since the opening of this important session, I have patiently awaited until now to speak on the grave problems which this house is called upon to discuss. I have deliberately taken time to observe what is taking place at present in this country and particularly to listen carefully to what is being said both here and among the electors at home. This will put me in a position, I trust, where I can express myself with more moderation, with greater impartiality and appropriateness.
As we look ahead, in this fourth year of the war, we find ourselves proceeding along a road to which there is as yet no visible ending; the horizon is hidden from us by the dense smoke arising from the most formidable struggle yet known in history.
Are we on the road to a victory which will reward us with happier days as a compensation for the sacrifices we have willingly accepted? I trust and believe this will be so. Will the road lead us on to material ruin whereby peace itself will be lost even while victory smiles upon us? I do not want to believe it, but like everyone else I am far from feeling reassured.
The problem which now confronts us is such that we should stop to ponder it. It is not by hiding our heads in the sand that we shall have a clear view of the situation. However, it seems to me that at this crucial stage all criticism should be constructive, that an}7 discussion made for the sole purpose of furthering political interests, playing upon popular emotions or attacking individuals who are not here to defend themselves should be banned from this house. Some may not see eye to eye with the government on certain matters, but I believe that merely destructive criticism, or blind and systematic opposition against the present government are calculated to injure our fellow-citizens' interests. That is why, like most of my colleagues who have been wrongly represented as being rebellious, I have so far wanted to remain in the ranks of the party which has sent me here, while reserving the right to oppose again any measure which I consider detrimental to the interests of my fellow-citizens and this country, as well as the right to agree with whatever good this government may do. I believe that only by fighting fearlessly for those principles which we consider just, by endeavouring to change the opinions of those who do not think as we do, and by remaining consistent with ourselves and faithful to our pledges we can make ourselves truly useful here.
Is not the endeavour to reform our own political party preferable to the creation of a new one? In order to destroy political partisanship which is so often discussed why should some people want to form a new party which, in turn, if it would endure, would have to foster partisanship? I do not regret the stand I have taken so far, as I feel that I enjoy the full support of the good people who elected me as their representative.
We are now discussing the budget for the coming fiscal year. In his speech, the hon. the Minister of Finance has told us frankly about the financial situation of this country. As could be expected in this time of war, the main object of the budget proposals is to obtain an unusual military contribution in terms of money. For the coming fiscal year an expenditure of about $5,500,000,000 is foreseen, and it is estimated that the revenue will amount to about $2,500,000,000; there will thus be a deficit of about $3,000,000,000, which will increase our debt by a like amount. Thus, on March 31, 1944. Canada's national debt will exceed 810,000,000.000, being about $1,000 per capita. These are staggering figures. Yet they bear out the situation in all its alarming simplicity. One has to be a great mathematician not to become dizzy at such a state of affairs and no doubt confronted by
The Budget-Mr. Lizotte

these figures our good people, like the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), and hon. members of this house, will lose all notions of the old dollar sign.
According to estimates, an additional 284 millions of dollars will accrue this j'ear from the income tax on individuals. It has been mentioned, quite seriously, by someone in the Progressive Conservative group that this must be an election budget on account of its being so mild. I hardly believe that the people will be very grateful over this election budget. It will rather be looked upon as a gift from the Greeks. In his speech, the official critic of the Conservative party (Mr. Harris, Danforth) has managed to blame this budget for not being heavy enough, saying that it falls short of a total war effort and that it does not call for all that the Canadian people can accomplish. Just think of it! Just imagine what it would be should his party be in power! After such extravagant language, one almost feels like thanking the Minister of Finance for his present gift.
In spite of present happenings, I say that the Canadian people will realize that they did well, in 1940, when they returned to office the party which is now directing our war effort instead of the extremists who would have caused strife and bloodshed had they succeeded in securing power. Last year, we have handed Great Britain a gift in war material and food aggregating a billion dollars, a step which I refused to countenance. We are now contemplating a grant of another billion dollars this year in favour of the allied nations and I reserve the right to object to such a measure. We have called to the colours about 800,000 men, organized a navy, air force and war industry of such tremendous proportions that they exceed all anticipations; still, we are told, in all earnestness, that our effort is insufficient, that our expenditures have not reached their proper level. It would be unbelievable had we not personally heard that statement.	'
I feel no hesitation in saying that I prefer the frankness with which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) honestly told us that the current budget was really heavy, that the taxes were truly high, even in comparison with what the Americans and Englishmen were called to Pay.
Fathers of large families will feel the pinch to a greater degree than others. Will they be able to bear this burden without the health and morale of themselves, their wives, and especially their young children being adversely affected? I am afraid not. They are the hardest hit and they are more numerous in

Quebec than in any other province; this is their reward for having given more children to their country. The minister's budget may well be considered as detrimental to the raising of families, unless some readjustment is made in favour of these fathers of numerous children.
What stand should we take on this budget when considered as a whole? To my mind some parts of it are good, others bad. I have just mentioned an evil which I detected in it. Here are some of its good points: the remission of half the tax on 1942 incomes, the imposition of certain new taxes as, for example, the tax on cigarettes and alcohol, which will, * I am sure, occasion no hardships to women and children. During the last war, the government in office had access to the imperial treasury for the financing of the war. It is true that the sums so advanced were repayable with interest. During the present conflict, not only does our own treasury finance our understakings, but it must also supply funds for the imperial treasury as well as that of some allied nations. Both situations must be compared if we are to get an adequate idea of the adventure we have launched upon at the present time. In all fairness, we must also compare the magnitude of the two wars in which we have been engaged in the course of the past twenty-five years. The conflict of 1914-18. was called the Great War; but what name shall we give to the present world war, to this universal slaughter which we are witnessing with a sense of horror?
At this time when our liberty is at stake, we are not always in agreement as to what action should be taken. Our opinions have been widely at variance, but I think there is a point on which we all agree and that is, the absolute necessity of winning this war if we want life to be worth living. The financial sacrifices imposed upon us are tremendous; they may at times involve certain irregularities and social injustice, but these are nothing compared to the air raids, and to the slaughter of the peoples subjected to the assaults of the enemy. May Divine Providence keep such bloody devastation away from our shores. It is far better to pay taxes, to produce goods, to work night and day, if necessary, in order to avoid these misfortunes, and accept, if not with cheerfulness, at least with Christian resignation, the necessary financial sacrifiecs which we are asked to make.
We have gone to war, we can no longer avoid what is inevitable. It is a fit and proper time to say: "the wine is drawn, it must be drunk." I am afraid we shall have to drain the cup to the dregs.

The Budget-Mr. Lizotle

We must, however, realize the situation without losing our heads and make the best of the situation we have to face. A well conceived war economy requires that the national revenue be sufficient to meet our war expenditures and to maintain our production. To achieve that end Canada must have a normal and well balanced distribution of its man-power resources. To ensure a fair distribution, the Department of Labour must take time to investigate conditions prevailing in our production services. It is in order that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) might have time for that investigation that, on the Address, I voted for the amendment of the hon. member for Riehelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin). Even men married before July, 1940, are now being called up. We might give thought to this problem calling for a better distribution of our man-power.
I am particularly interested in the problem as regards agriculture.
It is unfortunate, Mr. Speaker, that at a time when the allied nations are asking us to supply the food required for their sustenance and that of the armies fighting our battles, some of our Canadian farms are either idle or slowing down production for lack of experienced farm workers. This condition should not and indeed would not exist had we kept close watch upon the selective service machinery set up for that purpose. We should not have allowed the calling-up, under the Mobilization Act, of men essential to agriculture. Both publicly and privately, I have repeatedly urged the authorities concerned to grant these Tecruits a postponement of a permanent character for an indefinite period. Elsewhere, I have expressed the view that the Government ought to recognize, not by words, promises and advertisements in the newspapers, but by order in council, that agriculture is an essential industry and that experienced labour should be dealt with accordingly.
Conditions obtaining in my own constituency, which is essentially agricultural, surely exist also in other rural areas of this country.
The farmers' outlook is one of mistrust and misgivings, and not without reason. How do you expect a farmer, with the sole help of one or two sons, to undertake large scale production if he is hounded by the fear that his indispensable help will suddenly be taken away from him and called into the armed forces? The three and six month deferments hitherto allowed have been inadequate and have kept farmers in uncertaint3' and suspense. These
temporary extensions have deprived the farmer of his initiative and paralysed his courage and energy. I can sense it each time I come in contact with that worthy section of our population. There lies the main reason for the sluggishness and lessened efficiency in production.
It is however gratifying to realize that, this year, a wave of common sense seems to temper this frenzy of mass enlistments. From the ranks of the opposition, in and outside this house, we have had it dinned into our ears that the war effort amounted merely to building up large armed forces, and calling up men between the ages of 18 and 45 for the purpose of despatching them overseas. Those who dared to fight that crazy idea and who were in favour of a balanced war effort and of special treatment for the farm workers were called quitters. When these counsels of moderation were given by some one from the province of Quebec, he was called an isolationist, which was supposed to be the worst insult. What a fine revenge it is for all those who, like myself, have never ceased calmly to appraise the situation, without prejudice and in the interests of Canada, when they see our principal adversaries each in turn admit, in their speeches at least, that we were right. It must be admitted that we did not speak to the wind since those who did not want to listen to reason and who, in their morbid agitation, were ready to deprive Canada of her best workers, are now quieting down, retracing their steps, coming back to their senses, and asking that farmers' sons essential to agriculture be left on the farm. I suppose that the rationing of foodstuffs must have hit them in the right spot and inspired them with this wholesome conversion.
The government give us to understand, and I congratulate them in this regard, that they will ensure a more efficient co-ordination of our war effort in agriculture, industry and the armed forces through a better allocation of our man-power. At the beginning of February, the minister in charge of national selective service took the trouble to write to all mobilization boards in this country in order to tell them that the government's policy would tend to keep agricultural workers on farms, allowing them, after the working season, to accept temporary seasonal employment in lumbering or primary industries, provided they go back to farm work next season. That is an important concession we have secured. I hope we shall no longer meet with the difficulties we formerly had with the people whose duty it is to apply the Mobilization Act. Most of them, I readily admit, are well-intentioned,
The Budget-Mr. Lizotte

but their endeavours along the lines of tolerance and justice have often been hampered by the zeal of bureaucrats who are not accustomed to using their own judgment.

I would also like to discuss the fuel problem. A statement from the Department of Munitions and Supply has told us what w'e, who are from rural sections, already knew, namely, that the fuel situation has become alarming. In the town of Riviere du Loup where I live and which is close to huge timber limits, there has been a lack of cord wood during the coldest part of winter.
All lumber yards were empty and the St. Vincent de Paul society perforce levied a few logs here and there from private cellars containing barely sufficient stocks, so that large families might be kept from freezing. This scarcity was due to a lack of men for wood cutting operations. The dollar bonus granted by the government on each cord of fuel wood is good policy, but I would recommend extending the time until September. This particular work requires hands which must be found and the solution of this problem is up to the selective service if a part of our population is not to freeze to death next winter.
My allotted time precludes any discussion of farm problems which are not without importance. I will take the matter up on another occasion.
Frankly I do believe such claims as I have put forth are quite legitimate. I have no intention of embarrassing the government and my only wish is to make them fully acquainted with the legitimate feelings of the electors. Let the government, even in war time, follow a truly social and Canadian policy, let them implement their plans for the social security of our population in the post-war period, let them see that everyone is treated fairly, that the minority get its appropriate share, not only of responsibilities, but of rights as well, and thus the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) will be assured that harmony will easily be established at least among his supporters. This is the heartfelt hope of eveiy one of us.
On motion of Mr. Ross (Moose Jaw) the debate was adjourned.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
